EU leaders seek agreement on long-term budget and Ukraine at summit

November 26, 2026

Leaders of the EU's 27 member states are expected to thrash out the EU's budget for 2028 to 2034. Ukraine and European Central Bank leadership are also up for discussion. DW has more.

What you need to know

- Special European Council meeting for the next two days

- Details of long-term budget, Ukraine's 2027 financial needs and ECB leadership on the agenda

- Euro Summit also taking place with outgoing ECB President Christine Lagarde

You can follow developments from the EU summit taking place on Thursday 26th and Friday 27th November below:

EU budget from 2028 to 2034 and Ukraine funding on the agenda

European leaders are meeting for the next two days to thrash out a nearly €1.6 trillion ($1.76 trillion) budget proposal for 2028 to 2034.

The 27 member states are hoping to find common ground for a new budget proposal in the coming weeks and for members to agree on it at a summit on December 17 and 18.

"We, collectively, have the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead: boosting our competitiveness, strengthening our security and defence and projecting Europe in the world," said President of the European Council Antonio Costa ahead of the talks.

Costa outlined three key objectives for the next two days:

- to achieve a balanced distribution of funds between the EU's strategic priorities,

- to keep national contributions within reasonable limits

- to include a balanced basket of own resources, including five new sources of EU revenue

Revenue would come from digital services, non-recycled e-waste, tobacco related products, the carbon border adjustment mechanism and the emissions trading system, according to a statement from the European Council.

Ukraine's financing needs for 2027 and beyond will also be dealt with during talks. Currently, €45 billion has been earmarked in additional financial support for Ukraine in 2027, building on the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan for 2026 and 2027.

It's not expected to be a smooth process with Reuters quoting a diplomat as expecting "leaders to be yelling, complaining, showing they are willing to fight. They need that first. They need a breakdown, blood on the walls, before they can get to an agreement."

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the two-day Special European Council meeting in Brussels, which is expected to focus on the EU’s next long-term budget, support for Ukraine and then the leadership of the European Central Bank (ECB).

Leaders of the bloc's 27 members states will be looking to find common ground over the budget proposal for 2028 to 2034 ahead of an expected deal in December.

Continued support for Ukraine in 2027 and beyond is up for discussion as Russia's invasion drags on towards a fifth year.

The question of who replaces European Central Bank chief Christine Lagarde is also on the agenda.

Why it is here: Explains AI investment trends among wealthy Europeans

Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors.

The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman said 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors.

Goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The survey was carried out between June 29 and Aug. 18 this year.

The report on the findings, published Wednesday, did not specify the proportion of respondents who already have a stake in some kind of alternative investment — but wealthy Europeans appeared particularly bullish on the space.

Private equity made up the largest proportion of current alternatives holdings. Among wealthy Europeans with alternatives exposure, 62% said they invested in private equity. The second most commonly held asset class was private real estate, which was backed by 51% of European alternatives investors. Hedge funds were held by 37% of European alternatives owners, and private infrastructure was held by 30%.

One in four respondents who did not already own an alternative investment said they were likely to invest in the market in the coming 12 months. Among those already in the space, 26% said they were likely to increase their allocations over the next year, while just 5% said they planned to decrease their exposure.

Of the European investors who already owned alternatives, 54% said their assets had performed as expected, while 44% said their assets had exceeded their expectations to the upside. Only 2% said their alternative investments had performed worse than expected.

"Recent reforms gave individual investors unprecedented access to alternative asset classes like private equity, venture capital, and private credit," Kyle Kniffen, global head of alternatives for third-party wealth at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said in Wednesday's report.

He added that wealthy investors "look ready to jump at the opportunity."

"Our survey shows satisfaction among current alts owners is high and adoption looks set to increase," Kniffen said.

Alternative investments have increasingly become a staple of high-net-worth individuals' investment portfolios.

Over the past year, JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in the Asia-Pacific region have jumped 40%, while BNY Wealth says alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios — recently surpassing traditional assets for the first time.

But investing in alternatives carries risks. Private equity, for example, can lock up capital for long periods, and although the number of exits ticked slightly higher last year, the value of those deals fell.

Concerns about private credit, meanwhile, have dominated headlines, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warning on Oct. 14, 2025, that "cockroaches" were likely to be lurking in private markets.

— CNBC's Lee Ying Shan contributed to this article.

'Unacceptable': Major economies push back against new US tariffs

China, the European Union and other major trading partners on Thursday criticised new US tariffs of up to 20 percent proposed by US President Donald Trump after a probe into alleged global overcapacity, raising the prospect of fresh trade tensions with allies and rivals alike.

Major economies from China to the EU hit out at proposed new US tariffs after Washington concluded its months-long probe into alleged excess production, potentially opening a new phase in trade tensions with both allies and foes alike.

The new tolls, which follow an investigation launched days after the Supreme Court struck down US President Donald Trump's previous duties, range up to 20 percent and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners, with China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam in the crosshairs.

Some, such as Japan, denied having excessive production.

"Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity... It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this," the country's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals sought to take existing trade deals into account.

China is among those facing a 20-percent tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

"China understands that we're going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding," he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that Washington was offering China exemptions on around $30 billion of goods.

'Real concern'

The European Union said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the United States to stick by a deal struck last year.

"The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.

'Hollowing out'

The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on expenses to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.

Affordability was a key issue in this month's US midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both chambers of Congress by Democrats.

The announcement came as data showed the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge at a three-year high in October, adding to pressure to hike interest rates.

Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus said that he expected this probe to be among "the most important" actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and "never get turned off, even if there's no demand."

This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a "hollowing out" of US manufacturing, he added.

While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.

The new levies will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.

In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labor.

For economies facing both the forced labor and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack up and the higher rate will prevail, the US official said.

November 26, 2026

Here are the latest developments from India on Thursday, November 26:

- New Delhi urges US to work out trade-related within the structures of the ongoing trade deal talks

India seeks 'early conclusion' of trade deal with US

In its statement on planned new US tariffs, India's commerce ministry urged the US to resolve trade disputes and complete negotiations over a new trade deal.

The ministry said that it was "committed to working closely" with the US towards an "early conclusion" of the trade deal.

The US proposed a tariff rate of 25% on goods from India, reduced to 17% if a trade deal is reached.

The state of India-US trade deal negotiations

US President Donald Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi first announced talks for the US-India Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) last year.

But negotiations were delayed over strained ties and global conflict, reestablishing headway only this year.

The two nations released the framework for an interim trade agreement in February. As part of that deal, India would "eliminate or reduce tariffs" on all US industrial products and a range of US food and agricultural goods.

However, the negotiations for a final deal were once again stalled after the US Supreme Court invalidated much of Trump's sweeping global tariffs.

In October, India's Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman described the talks as having reached "a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult."

But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a few days later that New Delhi and Washington were "about asclose as you can be without having an executed agreement."

India rejects US charge of excess capacity

Facing a new United States tariff threat, India has stressed that any trade concerns be addressed within the framework of the ongoing trade deal talks between the two countries.

New Delhi's statement comes after Washington on Wednesday unveiled a new wave of tariffs on 14 of its major trade partners, including India, claiming that the economies were promoting excess industrial capacity.

"India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement. It has been India's position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations," a statement from New Delhi's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said late Wednesday.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced new import duties of 20% to 40% to counter the alleged excessive manufacturing abroad as it completed a monthslong probe into alleged unfair trade practices involving 16 trading partners.

The new tariffs will be subject to a period of public comment before taking effect.

"Today, after lengthy investigations, Ambassador Greer has determined that the acts, policies, and practices of various economies designed to artificially support manufacturing exports are unreasonable and burden or restrict US commerce and has proposed responsive action," the USTR said on Wednesday.

The USTR said that it will reduce the tariff rate for Indian imports to 17% if a trade deal is sealed between New Delhi and Washington in the long-drawn-out talks trade negotiations between the two sides.

India said that it had "engaged constructively" throughout USTR's investigation and said that it did not have "structural excess capacity in any sector."

Why it is here: Focuses on the impact of war and drought on Sudan's farmers

War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers

Attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan’s harvests and leaving millions without water.

Haider Mohamed has worked as a farmer in Sudan’s Northern State for more than 40 years, growing fava beans, wheat, and a variety of seasonal crops.

But Sudan’s water crisis – a combination of lower-than-average rainfall and war-induced devastation to infrastructure – has severely affected his harvest and his income.

It’s a situation Mohamed describes as unprecedented in his 40 years of farming.

Mohamed owns a small farm covering about four hectares (about 10 acres) in al-Saleem, near the city of Dongola. He keeps part of his harvest to feed his family, and then sells the rest at local markets to cover essential living expenses, including healthcare and his children’s education.

“Our crops were destroyed last year, and this year it is difficult to generate any income because we are still facing electricity and irrigation problems,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera, referring to drone attacks on power stations that disrupted electricity supplies, and regularly stopped him from using electricity-dependent irrigation systems. “We have accumulated a lot of debt, and we fear that we will not harvest enough to feed our children, let alone have any surplus to sell in the market.”

Mohamed’s experience is far from unique. Across Northern State and other parts of Sudan, water shortages caused by declining rainfall or disruptions to irrigation are increasingly threatening agricultural production and the livelihoods of farming communities.

“Those who rely on diesel-powered pumps [for irrigation] cannot find fuel, and when it is available, it is extremely expensive,” Mohamed explained. “We also cannot afford the cost of installing solar-powered irrigation systems. At this rate, no one will be able to continue farming in this country.”

The ongoing war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in 2023, has severely disrupted fuel supplies in the country. Attacks on Sudan’s largest oil refinery, as well as fuel depots and petrol stations, have exacerbated shortages.

In just October, attacks blamed on the RSF damaged critical infrastructure across 11 states, disrupting electricity and water services and disabling several water supply sources.

Rising global energy prices have also made imports more expensive, with the United Nations reporting that the price of diesel nearly doubled between March and August this year.

Struggle to find drinking water

In Sudan’s rain-fed agricultural regions, drought has compounded the problems facing farmers.

Rainfall during this year’s June-to-September rainy season declined across most of Sudan’s agricultural areas, believed to be linked to the ongoing global El Nino phenomenon. In the southeastern states of Gedaref and Sennar, rainfall was approximately 30 percent and 20 percent compared with normal levels, respectively, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

The two states normally account for about a quarter of Sudan’s sorghum production – the country’s main staple cereal.

The impact of the water crisis extends beyond the agricultural sector, affecting millions of people struggling to access drinking water and meet their basic household needs.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says damage to water and electricity systems and other civilian infrastructure has deprived millions of people of essential services, while disruptions to water supplies have increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

The UN children’s agency, UNICEF, estimates that more than 27 million people in Sudan are in need of water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance.

Between January and June of this year, UNICEF and its partners provided 6.6 million people with access to safe water, with approximately two-thirds of those receiving emergency assistance, including displaced people, those who had returned home and communities affected by conflict and cholera.

In the capital Khartoum, residents are still forced to stand in long queues for water, sometimes waiting for hours. Widespread disruptions to water supply networks and the shutdown of several water stations due to damage sustained during the war have left many households without a reliable water supply.

Saleh Zaki, who lives in Khartoum State’s East Nile district, said the area has suffered from water supply problems for many years, even before the outbreak of the war.

“Before the war, we repeatedly sought help from the authorities, only to be told there was no budget to address the problem,” Zaki said. “We therefore raised funds ourselves and hired a specialist to drill two wells, providing residents with limited water supply.”

“Since the conflict damaged the water networks … we urgently need more wells, repairs to the supply networks and solar-powered systems to support our neighbourhood and nearby communities,” he added.

Solar power

In August, the Sudanese government announced a series of measures designed to ease the water crisis and encourage families displaced by war to return home.

These measures include exempting solar panels imported for personal use from customs duties, taxes, and other government fees, and waiving residential water fees nationwide until the end of 2026.

However, these measures remain limited in their impact unless accompanied by broader economic policies.…

EU leaders face showdown over Ukraine funding as divisions deepen

European Union leaders on Thursday are set to tackle deep divisions as they meet in Brussels to discuss the bloc's long-term budget in Brussels, which includes a proposed €45 billion loan to keep Ukraine funded through 2027.

European Union (EU) leaders will seek on Thursday to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree on a significant new loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year.

The new joint budget is a statement of the EU’s ambitions in the world and is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. The 2028-2034 package could amount to between 1% and 1.2% of the bloc’s gross national income.

“The time has come to reach an agreement,” European Council President António Costa wrote in a summit invitation letter. Last weekend, he tabled a new proposal to solve the budget riddle, cutting about 10% off the original European Commission plan.

Costa, who will chair the two-day meeting in Brussels, said that leaders have “the responsibility to find a balanced agreement that will allow the European Union to take on the challenges ahead.”

Complicating things are upcoming elections in France, Italy and Poland next year and in Spain on Sunday. The hard right leads in surveys in France and winners in Poland and Spain are tough to predict. New governments could make it even harder to agree on a deal next year if one isn't found by the end of next month.

The EU is divided into hard-to-move camps when it comes to the budget. They’re getting even tougher to budge as Europe’s debt strife spreads and countries are forced into greater defense spending over Russia’s almost five-year-long war on Ukraine.

Around a third of countries are so-called net contributors that pay in more than they get back in allocations. Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden are the most vocal in their opposition to being asked to cough up even more and demand belt-tightening.

A large group of countries, led by France and Italy and dubbed the “friends of cohesion,” staunchly defends funds that protect farmers and pay for infrastructure projects in relatively poor member countries, to help bring them up to EU standards.

Those policies make up about two thirds of the entire budget.

But most countries also want to direct spending to new areas, as the EU confronts challenges like supporting Ukraine as it fights off a Russian invasion and remaining competitive in the face of high energy prices and trade tensions with the US and China.

It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data and could amount to 5 billion euros ($5.5 billion) a year.

Ukraine is a big part of the budget puzzle. The spending package foresees a 100 billion-euro ($110 billion) envelope for Ukraine over seven years. The leaders must also decide on a new 45 billion-euro ($49.4 billion) loan for the country.

Earlier this month, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if there were no “collective commitment” made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception.”

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. In a letter to Costa, Merz said that helping “Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros ($99 billion) to cover most of the Ukrainian government's needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

Why it is here: Reports on SpaceX's plan for space-based data centers

FCC says SpaceX can deploy 1 million satellites for data centers in space. Scientists are skeptical

The Trump administration on Wednesday gave SpaceX the green light to deploy 1 million satellites that it said would create data centers in space, a long-lofty goal of Elon Musk's rocket company, in a move that has raised both skepticism and alarm among some scientists.

The U.S. Federal Communications Commission lauded its authorization as a historic first amid the artificial intelligence race. It said that SpaceX's one million "orbital compute modules" (forming a data center constellation called "Starmind") would process massive amounts of data that would be used back on Earth — and bring humans closer to harnessing "the full power of the sun."

"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, who was appointed by Republican President Donald Trump, said in a statement. He added that Wednesday's move "opens a bold new frontier."

A lengthier authorization order published by the FCC noted that the company must deploy at least "one authorized space station" by 2033 — and then gradually add more and more through 2040. Musk welcomed the decision over social media.

The world's richest man has long vowed to form vast, solar-powered data centers in space to help run AI tools on Earth. But scientists and industry experts have stressed enormous technical and financial obstacles, as well as a host of environmental concerns.

Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites into space to create data centers "a fantasy."

"It's not going to happen," he said Wednesday.

Proponents of data centers in space argue that capturing the sun's energy would ease pressure on power grids and cut demand for sprawling computing warehouses on Earth (and resources like water needed to cool them). Space seems to offer a solution because it is cold, but it is also a vacuum, trapping heat inside objects much like a thermos. Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to otherwise radiating that heat out — and sending lots of smaller satellites could potentially carry the necessary material combined, but it would be expensive and difficult.

He and others also point to additional risks, such as atmospheric pollution through launches and reentries, as well as possible in-orbit collisions that could impact other essential satellites.

"You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," said Becker, noting such crashes could create "a cloud of debris" in the low Earth orbit — where many weather and telecommunication satellites are also found.

In its ruling, the FCC maintained that SpaceX's proposed Starmind constellation operates consistently with its orbital debris rules. It also acknowledged that it had received a "substantial number" of public comments leading up to its authorization Wednesday, including petitions to deny SpaceX's request. But the regulator maintained that deploying the satellites "serves the public interest" — and said that it dismissed topics that it didn't have authority over, such as environmental concerns.

The American Astronomical Society, satellite communication company Viasat and Amazon-owned Kuiper Systems were among those who called on the regulator to deny SpaceX's proposed data centers in space.

In a statement Wednesday, the AAS said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the FCC's decision. The organization said that SpaceX's proposed position of data centers in low Earth orbit would undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky."

"The proposed constellation involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects," AAS said, noting that "these satellites would therefore be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky."

Becker echoed that sentiment. "It also is pollution of the night sky to the naked eye," he said.

Viasat, Amazon, SpaceX and the FCC did not immediately respond to The Associated Press' requests for further comment Wednesday.

Why it is here: Opinion piece on nuclear abolition and the risk of nuclear catastrophe

The world must choose between nuclear abolition and nuclear catastrophe

The upcoming UN nuclear ban treaty conference offers an opportunity to challenge the dogma of nuclear deterrence.

The world is currently facing the greatest risk of deliberate or inadvertent nuclear conflict since the Cold War – or perhaps ever.

While the threat of nuclear war may have dropped out of the headlines, it did not go away with the end of the Cold War. The United States and Russia had a window of opportunity in the early 1990s to eliminate nuclear weapons when there were still only 5 nuclear powers, but they spurned it.

Fast forward to today, and these two countries that, between them, possess almost 90 percent of the world’s nuclear weapons have initiated wars with non-nuclear-armed countries: Ukraine and Iran. The aggressors’ leaders, presidents Putin and Trump, have made threats to use nuclear weapons.

It is worrying that while these threats have not gone unreported, they have quickly passed from the headlines. However, the good news is that the rest of the world is pushing back against this ongoing existential threat – not through mass protests, but through quiet, multilateral diplomacy and persistent advocacy by civil society, including my organisation, ICAN.

Putin and Trump did recently meet their Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, who commands the third-largest nuclear arsenal, for their first-ever three-way summit. They reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. But in their declaration, they did not say anything new; simply that they would discuss reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

The question we face today of how we ensure our security in a world of newly competing nuclear-armed powers is, at its root, the same we have faced since the development of the atomic bomb – how do we deal with the constant threat these weapons pose to humanity?

Despite the insistence of the nuclear-armed minority that there is no alternative to their theory of nuclear deterrence, we are part of a diplomatic push offering the world a choice. Powerful countries can continue to blindly believe in deterrence dogma, a theory of human behaviour unsupported by evidence, that has led us to the brink of catastrophe more than once. Or countries can agree to the total elimination of these weapons for good.

Deterrence is based on the capability and willingness to use nuclear weapons to kill millions of innocent people. The threat is present every moment in the form of the 4,000 nuclear weapons deployed and ready to use at short notice – more than enough to end civilisation as we know it many times over. This is the current choice of a minority of countries – the nine that have nuclear weapons and their nuclear-endorsing allies, principally the members of NATO.

The alternative of abolishing nuclear weapons is growing in strength, but not talked about nearly as much. It is the choice of the majority of the world and is embodied in the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons – the United Nations’ nuclear ban treaty, or TPNW, that 101 countries have already signed or ratified.

The treaty bans nuclear weapons and all activities associated with them outright and has created a new norm of international law that makes these weapons unacceptable, alongside biological and chemical weapons.

The first review conference of the treaty will soon take place at the UN in New York under the presidency of South Africa – a country that set the example of how nuclear weapons can be eliminated by doing it. In the 1970s, Apartheid South Africa, with the help of Israel, developed a nuclear arsenal, but then voluntarily dismantled it under international supervision in the 1990s.

The conference will evaluate how the treaty has been implemented so far and identify how it can be further strengthened. Unlike the review conference of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty earlier this year that failed to reach consensus for the third consecutive time, this gathering is expected to agree on a number of significant decisions. There will be a strong political declaration stressing the importance of nuclear disarmament and the urgency of addressing the growing risk that nuclear weapons could be used again in conflict, including calling out the role of nuclear deterrence in driving this threat to all countries. There is also the prospect of more countries using the conference as an opportunity to sign or ratify the treaty.

As TPNW states have noted, deterrence does not bring security and stability; it brings chronic insecurity to the entire world. There is nothing inevitable about nuclear weapons. They are a political choice. They are created by human hands, and they can be dismantled by human hands – as South Africa demonstrated.

The remaining countries that support the treaty but still need to join it should do so now. That will highlight just how isolated the nine nuclear-armed countries are and add to the pressure on them and their allies to get on the right side of history.

The words of President Kennedy addressing the UN 65 years ago remain as relevant today: “The weapons of war must be abolished before they abolish us.”

Dragonflies feast on other insects during autumn migrations

Dragonflies feast on a host of insects—and each other—during their autumn migrations, new research shows. Scientists studied dragonflies at the Pass of Bujaruelo—a 30-meter (98-foot) gap between two high peaks in the Pyrenees, through which millions of insects migrate every year.

By analyzing DNA from the guts of two dragonfly species, the researchers identified a wide range of prey and found dragonflies eat other migrating insects.

The findings reveal a previously hidden "aerial food web," with dragonflies acting as important predators as insects move across landscapes and international borders. The paper, published in the journal Ecography, is titled "Migratory insect flows structure trophic interactions in dragonfly diets."

"We tend to view migrations as a stream of animals moving—but we don't often consider the interactions between them," said Dr. Eva Jimenez-Guri, from the Center for Ecology and Conservation on Exeter's Penryn Campus in Cornwall.

"Our findings show that migration concentrates many species, creating new opportunities for predators and prey to interact."

DNA reveals a varied in-flight diet

Both dragonfly species in the study—the lesser emperor and the common darter—are known to catch prey in flight.

By catching dragonflies at the pass and analyzing their gut contents using a process called DNA metabarcoding, the researchers found:

- Eighty-seven different prey species had been eaten.

- Flies (Diptera) were found in every dragonfly and made up the largest proportion of their diet overall.

- 90% of lesser emperor dragonflies and 70% of darters had eaten species that are known to migrate.

- Crop pest species, including the bean seed fly, were among the species eaten—highlighting the importance of dragonflies for agriculture.

- Some lesser emperors had eaten larger migratory prey, including clouded yellow butterflies.

- The diets of lesser emperors included their smaller dragonfly cousins, the darters.

Dragonflies prey on fellow travelers

"The real surprise for us was that almost all gut samples from lesser emperors contained smaller darter dragonflies," said Dr. Karl Wotton.

"We know that dragonflies prey on each other as nymphs (a juvenile stage when they live in water) but we didn't expect this interaction to appear so consistently in adults traveling along the same route.

"Our results reveal multiple levels of predators and prey traveling together. This is not simply a stream of insects moving south. It is part of a much larger food web moving through the sky."

World's fastest animal could nearly double its livable territory by 2080 in the UK due to climate change

The area suitable for peregrine falcons within the UK could grow by 74% by the year 2080 under a high-emissions climate scenario, a new study has shown.

This expansion could in principle allow these apex predators to establish more breeding territories. But more suitable area doesn't automatically lead to more birds, warns the author: active conservation and protection interventions are also needed. Furthermore, the picture isn't rosy across the board: habitat for other established species of raptors is on track to decline in the UK unless mitigating measures are taken in time.

"Breeding British birds of prey may respond very differently to future climate change," said Dr. Connor T. Panter, a researcher within the School of Geography at the University of Nottingham and the author of the study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution.

"Conditions associated with peregrine falcons elsewhere in Europe may become more favorable in the UK under climate change. The area suitable for hen harriers is likewise predicted to expand, while white-tailed eagles and short-eared owls may experience reductions in suitable areas."

Bird's-eye view

Boasting a diversity of raptors is often a hallmark of a healthy, well-balanced ecosystem. By regulating the numbers of small mammals, these species can prevent overgrazing, habitat erosion and the loss of plant biodiversity. Today, five species of owls and 15 species of daytime raptors such as hawks, ospreys and buzzards breed in the UK.

Most suffered devastating declines in the mid-20th century due to the widespread use of organochlorine insecticides, which accumulated in raptors to catastrophic effect.

When the EU banned these compounds from the mid-1970s onward, populations of many raptors tended to bounce back. Nevertheless, the British Trust for Ornithology estimates that the UK's breeding population of peregrine falcons decreased by 57% between 1995 and 2024 due to illegal persecution, declines in available prey and avian flu. Currently, the UK has between 1,750 and 1,800 pairs of peregrines.

Panter aimed to predict changes in environmental suitability across the UK for 16 breeding raptor species under two IPCC emissions scenarios: the "middle-of-the-road" socioeconomic pathway SSP2–4.5 and the "worst-case" SSP5–8.5 pathway. Input for the projections came from "niche models" fitted around 14 environmental variables, including temperature range, various measures of precipitation, elevation and the percentage of land covered by five types of habitat.

Not simply winners versus losers

The results showed that the UK area suitable for peregrine falcons could expand from 110,257 km² (42,600 square miles) today to 155,000 km² (59,800 square miles) (+40.6%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and to 191,319 km² (73,900 square miles) (+73.5%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080.

The area suitable for hen harriers could increase from 74,835 km² (28,900 square miles) today to 96,025 km² (37,100 square miles) (+28.3%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and to 105,553 km² (40,800 square miles) (+41.0%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080. The golden eagle, little owl, long-eared owl, western barn owl and western marsh harrier were likewise predicted to see area increases, albeit by smaller amounts.

The bad news is that the habitat of British short-eared owls, red kites, merlins and Eurasian goshawks is expected to shrink considerably. The white-tailed eagle appears to be worst affected, with suitable habitat potentially disappearing from the UK: namely, a reduction in area from 2,306 km² (890 square miles) today to 444 km² (171 square miles) (-80.7%) under SSP2–4.5 by 2060, and only 65 km² (25 square miles) (-97.2%) under SSP5–8.5 by 2080.

In contrast, the area suitable for the common buzzard, European sparrowhawk and tawny owl didn't change by much under any of the models.

Panter concluded that different species are likely to respond in different ways to climate change: the range of outcomes is thus more varied than simply a tally of winners and losers. But what can ordinary people do to help preserve a healthy abundance and diversity of birds of prey in spite of these conflicting trends?

"It is important for everyone to play their part in conserving raptors. This means reducing threats to birds of prey, including shooting and trapping, poisoning, and collisions with human infrastructure such as power lines and wind turbines," said Panter.

"Improving habitat connectivity and preserving existing habitats for both raptors and their prey is equally important. People can also contribute by participating in citizen science programs, such as iNaturalist, where sharing wildlife observations helps scientists better understand and monitor species as their environments change."

item.title: Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?
item.description:

Sending an Australian astronaut to space is expensive. How do we work out if it's worth it?

Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg—who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024—would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut.

To "buy a seat" on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark.

There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a homegrown astronaut to space could benefit industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space.

However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it's costly. As we're in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine, it's crucial to properly analyze some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal.

What counts as an Australian astronaut?

The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately.

The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space. But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn't been given the label of the first "female Australian astronaut."

The federal government hasn't signaled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science Minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal "reckless."

These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then-Science Minister Barry Jones noted it wasn't a high priority. Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in.

The cost would be substantial

We don't know if Australians would support spending $100 million on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut program, but respondents were not given a cost.

Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs, public support decreases. When asked in 2023, more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canceled.

Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently, the Australian Space Agency's funding is $21.7 million over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund the agency for a decade.

Put another way, $100 million is half of the total government investment in space or space-adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occur at universities, in government agencies and in private industry; many organizations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply.

Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There's no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming. An astronaut can't meet all these needs, and we don't know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn't have a whole-of-government space policy, and an astronaut is not a space program.

The suggestion that Australia's growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space?

ESA has a geographic return policy under which member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state and is not looking to become one.

The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it's difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based.

What about inspiration?

Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg's selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country.

However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM.

The selection process was not nationally competitive, and there's no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg's footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space.

We shouldn't ignore the fact that many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it's exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy—after all, we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sports—but we should also recognize that many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space.

Unanswered questions remain

If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are—to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for.

A key final question is: What next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but it also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut.…

Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea

- Date:

November 25, 2026

- Source:

University of Miami Rosenstiel School of Marine, Atmospheric, and Earth Science

- Summary:

More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

- Share:

More than a mile below the surface of the Red Sea, researchers from the University of Miami (UM) Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science discovered rare deep-sea brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern extension of the Red Sea. These unusually salty underwater lakes could provide clues to how Earth's oceans formed millions of years ago and help guide the search for life on other planets.

The discovery was made by Sam Purkis, professor and chair of the UM Department of Marine Geosciences, and his colleagues in collaboration with OceanX. The researchers located the pools at a depth of more than one mile (1,770 meters) using a remotely operated underwater vehicle (ROV) deployed from the OceanXplorer, an advanced research vessel equipped to investigate some of the least accessible environments on Earth.

"Until we understand the limits of life on Earth, it will be difficult to determine if alien planets can host any living beings," said Purkis. "Our discovery of a rich community of microbes that survive in extreme environments can help trace the limits of life on Earth and can be applied to the search for life elsewhere in our solar system and beyond."

Life thrives in extreme underwater lakes

Brine pools rank among the harshest environments on our planet. Their waters contain exceptionally high concentrations of salt, feature unusual chemical conditions, and are completely devoid of oxygen. Despite these seemingly inhospitable conditions, the pools support abundant microbial life. Previous research on microbes inhabiting Red Sea brine pools has even identified biologically active molecules with potential anticancer properties.

The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, mark the first documented discovery of brine pools in the Gulf of Aqaba. Remarkably, the researchers nearly missed them.

"We were very lucky," said Purkis. "The discovery came in the last five minutes of the ten-hour ROV dive that we could dedicate to this project."

Hidden records of ancient tsunamis and earthquakes

Beyond their biological significance, the pools serve as natural archives of the region's geological history. Situated relatively close to the coastline, their extremely salty waters and absence of oxygen help preserve evidence of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that occurred in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. Regional tectonic activity has produced numerous faults and fractures across the seabed in this part of the gulf.

Earlier in 2022, Purkis and his colleagues uncovered evidence of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that likely generated a substantial tsunami. Understanding the region's history of such events could have important implications for coastal development in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

The study, titled "Discovery of the deep-sea NEOM Brine Pools in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea," was published on June 27, 2022, in Communications Earth & Environment.

The research team included Sam J. Purkis, Hannah Shernisky, Peter K. Swart, Arash Sharifi, Amanda Oehlert, Gaëlle Duchâtellier, James Klaus, Gregor P. Eberli, Larry Peterson, and Graham Kolodziej from the UM Rosenstiel School; Fabio Marchese and Francesca Benzoni from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology's Red Sea Research Center; Giovanni Chimienti from the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy; Andrew Craig and Mattie Rodrigue from OceanX; Jürgen Titschack from MARUM -- Center for Marine Environmental Sciences in Germany; and Ameer Abdulla from NEOM.

NEOM, a company developing the Saudi Arabian coastline, provided funding for the four-week research expedition aboard the OceanXplorer.

item.description:

Astronomers may have discovered a black hole born before the first stars

- Date:

November 25, 2026

- Source:

Universe Today

- Summary:

A mysterious object named Phoebe, detected when it briefly magnified a distant star, could be a primordial black hole formed just after the Big Bang. With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

- Share:

On December 18, 2019, astronomers recorded something unusual happening to a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. For approximately one hour, the star gradually grew brighter before fading back to its usual appearance. The change was smooth and symmetrical, with no sudden explosion or flare. It looked as though an invisible object had moved between Earth and the star, bending its light in our direction. Afterward, the star returned to normal and showed no further changes in brightness.

Researchers have named the mysterious object Phoebe, but its true identity remains unknown. The event appears to be an example of gravitational microlensing, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein's general theory of relativity. When a compact object with sufficient mass passes in front of a distant star, its gravity bends the star's light and temporarily magnifies its brightness. This produces a recognizable pattern that differs from the changes caused by variable stars, stellar flares, or passing asteroids.

Astronomers at Swinburne University in Melbourne identified the signal while examining observations from a survey that frequently monitored stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. The distinctive pattern convinced the team that they had detected a genuine gravitational microlensing event. What remained uncertain was the nature of the invisible object responsible.

Three Possible Explanations for the Mysterious Object

Researchers have identified three potential explanations for Phoebe. One possibility is a rogue planet that was expelled from its original solar system and now travels alone through the Milky Way. Another is a similar wandering planet located within the Large Magellanic Cloud. If the second explanation proves correct, Phoebe would become the first planet discovered through gravitational microlensing beyond our galaxy.

The third possibility is far more extraordinary. Phoebe could be a primordial black hole, an ancient object that formed in the earliest moments of the universe. Unlike ordinary black holes, which develop when massive stars collapse, primordial black holes could have emerged from extremely dense regions of space during the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang. Such objects would have formed long before the first stars appeared.

A One-Hour Signal Reveals a Surprising Clue

The unusually short duration of the brightening provides an important clue about Phoebe's mass. Gravitational microlensing events depend partly on how massive the intervening object is. Generally, lighter objects produce shorter events, although their speed and position also influence how long the magnification lasts.

Phoebe's signal lasted approximately 60 minutes, placing it near the detection limit of current astronomical surveys. Using the observed duration and their models of the event, researchers estimated that the object has a mass roughly three times that of the Moon. That would make it considerably less massive than any planet in our solar system and far too small to be a conventional black hole formed by a collapsing star.

Black holes produced through stellar collapse typically have masses of at least about five times that of the Sun. Phoebe's estimated mass falls enormously below that threshold. If the mysterious object really is a black hole, its tiny mass would point toward a primordial origin rather than the death of a star.

Could Phoebe Be a Primordial Black Hole Linked to Dark Matter?

To investigate where Phoebe might belong, the researchers compared the likelihood that the object originated from different populations. These included stars in the Milky Way, stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and objects associated with the surrounding dark matter halo.

The results strongly favored the dark matter halo. According to the team's calculations, Phoebe is approximately 100,000 times more likely to belong to this population than to one associated with ordinary stellar matter. This enormous difference makes a potential connection to dark matter particularly intriguing, although it does not establish that Phoebe is a primordial black hole.

If the primordial black hole interpretation is correct, Phoebe could be among the oldest objects ever detected. It may have formed before the first atoms and stars existed, when the universe was still experiencing the extreme conditions that followed the Big Bang.

For roughly 13 billion years, such an object could have traveled unseen through space, leaving almost no trace of its existence. Then, on a single night in December 2019, its gravity may have briefly magnified the light of a distant star, offering astronomers a remarkable glimpse of something born near the very beginning of the universe.

Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

Robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Greater Precision Does Not Improve Recovery

Twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.

The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, said: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an important step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement."

Professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, said: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. Professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, said: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. Why it is here: Clear reporting on Medicare changes affecting specialists, with real-world impact on patient care.

Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.

But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.

It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.

“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.

Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.

“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”

These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.

The cuts to payment rates for same-day services were slated to be 50% when first proposed in 2018, before backlash from physicians and patients softened the blow. Under the final rule, effective Jan. 1, 2027, Medicare will pay for the highest-valued same-day service at 100%, then reduce payment for each additional service rendered on the same day by 20% when physicians perform evaluations and other routine outpatient services. CMS argues the lowered rate is justified because providers use less resources — for patient registration, scheduling, and support, for example — when patients are seen and treated on the same day at the same practice.

Amy Hunsberger, a lawyer with Manatt, a legal advisory and consultancy, said the cuts are partly motivated by the statutory requirement that physician payments cannot increase without Congressional approval, forcing Medicare to cut back on expenses as the agency spends more on health care costs.

“You have a balloon that has so much air in it, and when you reduce payment in one area of services, you’re squeezing the balloon on one side, and it pushes payments out to the rest of the balloon,” said Hunsberger. “This balloon is not updated for inflation and relies on continual, almost annual congressional bailouts to get clinicians to some semblance of reasonable payment.”

Because these policy changes apply to the number of claims relating to health care services rendered on the same day and to any specific specialty, it’s unclear how they will impact Medicare beneficiaries. The American Parkinson Disease Association said patients with Parkinson’s disease are worried that it could impact their ability to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain.

McGuire estimates that the policy change will decrease her profits by 6%. The policy goes into effect on Jan. 1. She doesn’t know how much longer her practice will last.

“There are times where I ask myself if I should just close up shop and call it a day, and go find a job at Trader Joe’s or Starbucks, where I can have a reliable income,” she said. “If it wasn’t for the fact that medicine has always been a calling for me and the joy it brings me to take care of patients, I probably would have done that already. But I’m also getting to the point where I don’t think this is financially viable and a long-term solution.”

One body, two systems: Integrating dental and medical care dramatically improves dental follow-up

In the United States, medical and dental care are traditionally separate. Care is provided in separate locations, recorded in separate systems and paid for via separate methods.

But a new study has found that bringing the two systems together dramatically improves kids' odds of dental follow-up, creating new opportunities to prevent oral disease.

Integrating dental care with medical care resulted in 30%–60% greater odds of continuing dental care, and patients at an integrated clinic had significantly better dental health.

"We asked: Are kids more likely to return for dental care in this integrated environment?" says Jeri Bullock, D.D.S., M.S., associate dean for clinical affairs at the University of Utah School of Dentistry and first author on the study. "We found that yes, they were. Definitely."

The results are published in the Journal of Dental Research.

Care under one roof increases dental checkups and improves health

Researchers compared dental care follow-up between two dental clinics in Salt Lake City: Liberty Elementary Clinic, where medical and dental care are provided by two different organizations with separate health records, and South Main Clinic, where medical and dental care are fully integrated. By tracking over 1,600 pediatric visits to the two clinics, the team found that kids who visited the fully integrated South Main Clinic were 30%–60% more likely to return for a dental appointment within two years.

Importantly, kids who got dental care at South Main tended to have healthier teeth despite demographic differences—such as a trend toward lower socioeconomic status—that often correlate with worse health outcomes. This suggests that an integrated system may lower structural barriers to dental care, helping all children get the care they need.

Researchers suspect that the better oral health of South Main patients is driven by their more frequent dentist appointments.

"The oral health-related quality of life is much higher for patients visiting that site," says Brenda Heaton, Ph.D., associate dean for research at the University of Utah School of Dentistry and senior author on the study. "They're getting the same kind of care at both sites, but because of the model of care delivery, they have better outcomes."

For patients and families used to separate dental care, full medical-dental integration is a big change.

"It's a very unique experience for a patient to be able to get both their medical care and their dental care under the same roof," Heaton says. "Imagine it's a primary care visit for pediatrics, and the kid shares with the physician that they have pain in their mouth. When they check out, the front desk can schedule a dental appointment for them right there at the clinic." Medical and dental health records are also shared on the same electronic system. And if needed, a dentist can walk right down the hall to do a quick consultation during a general checkup.

Dentists and dental researchers have advocated for increased integration into health care systems for years, but the rigorous statistics of the new study make its results especially compelling, the team says. Researchers used multiple parallel methods of data analysis to facilitate direct comparisons between demographically similar patients, allowing them to isolate the effect of medical-dental integration. "It allowed us to really compare apples to apples," Bullock says.

Seeing results in the real world

Bullock adds that the results bear out what she's seen in her own clinical practice at South Main. "I see this day to day," Bullock says. "I know this works; I'm seeing these kids back. I just felt that there was something special. But to actually see it come out in the numbers was really gratifying. I was really excited and proud and felt good as a clinician that what I felt and what I was seeing was true to what the data was saying."

The team warns that the barriers to full medical-dental integration are significant. Bullock notes that effective integration needs a unified electronic health record system, so that dentists and pediatricians can quickly understand a patient's medical needs and provide seamless care. Transitioning to such a system represents a major hurdle for most medical systems.

Still, the researchers are hopeful that their results might help drive greater integration and better patient care, both at University of Utah clinics and more broadly.

"For more than a century, we've treated one body through two disconnected systems," Heaton says. "When medical and dental care work together, we reduce barriers, simplify care for families and create more opportunities to prevent disease before it becomes a larger health problem. My hope is that studies like this help move health care toward models that recognize oral health as an integral part of overall health."

Half of adults in long COVID study report difficulty breathing 4 years later

Half of adults in a new long COVID study reported symptoms that suggested dysfunctional breathing more than four years after their initial infection. Those with persistent breathing problems tended to be younger and female, and they were less likely to be hospitalized during acute COVID infection.

Dysfunctional breathing is an umbrella term for altered or abnormal breathing patterns such as rapid or shallow breathing that can lead to shortness of breath. The condition is associated with a high long COVID symptom burden overall.

For the study, published in Respiratory Research, a team led by researchers at Karolinska University Hospital in Stockholm, Sweden, analyzed data from 288 participants diagnosed as having long COVID.

Of those, half (143) had dysfunctional breathing four years after their initial COVID infection, as indicated by elevated Nijmegen questionnaire (NQ) scores. The NQ is a self-reported screening tool used to assess functional respiratory symptoms. NQ scores range from 0 to 64 and, for this study, an elevated score was defined as 23 or greater.

38% reported rapid heart rate upon standing

At an initial baseline visit after getting COVID (May 2020 to December 2022), participants who later scored 23 or above on the NQ walked significantly shorter distances on the six-minute walking test than those with lower scores, completed fewer repetitions on a one-minute sit-to-stand test and had weaker muscle contraction when inhaling. Standard lung-function measures were similar between groups.

At the 2024 follow-up, participants who were not hospitalized during acute COVID infection had about six times higher odds of scoring 23 or above on the NQ. Younger age, greater shortness of breath at the initial assessment and a lower volume of air exhaled in the first second of a lung-function test were also independent predictors of dysfunctional breathing.

Factors independently associated with higher odds of scoring 23 or above at follow-up include more severe shortness of breath and more long COVID and depression symptoms. Thirty-eight percent of those with scores of 23 and above reported a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), compared with 8% in those with lower scores. A higher proportion of those with NQ scores of 23 and greater were on sick leave than those with lower scores (44% vs. 14%).

POTS causes an abnormally rapid heart rate when moving from lying down or sitting to standing up, with no substantial drop in blood pressure.

Need for studies combining patient-reported, objective measures

The response rate at follow-up was moderate, note the researchers, and nonresponse bias can't be ruled out. "Individuals with ongoing symptoms may have been more likely to participate, while those without persistent symptoms may have been less likely to respond to the follow-up survey," they write. At the same time, those with severe symptoms may be underrepresented because the burden of completing the follow-up questionnaire was too great.

They conclude, "These findings demonstrate a substantial burden of persistent functional respiratory complaints but should not be interpreted as evidence of clinically confirmed dysfunctional breathing." They call for future studies that combine patient-reported assessments with objective measures of breathing patterns and lung function.

Ecuadorian plant shows potential to control bacteria in food

A plant traditionally used by Indigenous communities in Ecuador could have a new application: helping control bacteria in ready-to-eat foods. A study published in the journal Foods found that extracts of Piper carpunya, locally known as guaviduca, reduced the presence of Clostridium perfringens in a refrigerated risotto food model.

The extract prepared using a mixture of water and ethanol reduced bacterial levels approximately 100-fold compared with contaminated food without the extract. Previous research had already identified antimicrobial activity in P. carpunya, but its effectiveness when incorporated directly into food had yet to be evaluated.

The research team tested three types of extracts obtained from the plant's leaves against 20 microorganisms associated with foodborne illnesses and food spoilage. Eight microorganisms showed some degree of susceptibility, including C. perfringens, a bacterium capable of producing toxins and causing food poisoning.

The researchers then moved beyond laboratory testing by incorporating the most promising extracts into precooked risotto, which was stored at 5°C for 30 days. Some samples were deliberately inoculated with C. perfringens to determine whether the antimicrobial effect could be maintained within the food.

The most significant result was observed with the hydroethanolic extract, prepared using equal parts ethanol and water. In the contaminated risotto, it produced an approximately 2-log reduction in C. perfringens levels compared with the control group by day seven, equivalent to a roughly 100-fold decrease. From day 15 onward, the bacterium was no longer detectable in those samples.

The same extract also reduced other bacterial groups used as indicators of food spoilage. "Our aim is to develop natural additives that offer functionality similar to that of artificial additives, while allowing their incorporation into clean-label products," said Felipe Reyes Bueno, a researcher at Universidad Técnica Particular de Loja (UTPL) and an author of the study. Although previous studies had identified antioxidant properties in P. carpunya extracts, the extracts exhibited a pro-oxidant effect when incorporated into risotto.

Nevertheless, malondialdehyde concentrations, an indicator of lipid oxidation, remained below 0.35 mg/kg throughout the 30-day storage period, lower than levels associated with perceptible rancidity. P. carpunya is not yet ready for use as a food preservative. The study was conducted using a risotto food model with an extract concentration of 8% and did not include chemical characterization or sensory evaluation of the extracts.

The researchers now aim to identify the compounds responsible for the observed antimicrobial activity, optimize the concentration required to achieve the desired effect and assess how the extract influences the taste and other sensory characteristics of the food. "We still need to study the stability of the extracts, further refine the experiment and investigate in greater depth the extraction methods for the compounds responsible for this antimicrobial activity," the researcher added.

Participants expressed strong interest in an intervention that could help them improve their overall health, build healthy eating and cooking skills and receive guidance and accountability from a registered dietitian.

The findings highlighted the importance of culturally relevant recruitment materials featuring Black adults across ages, genders and body sizes, along with appealing healthy foods and the technology used in the intervention. Participants also emphasized that dietitians should understand Black cultural food traditions and lived experiences, noting that cultural competence was more important than the dietitian's race alone.

"Engaging Black adults in nutrition research requires more than simply sharing information about a study," said lead investigator Loneke T. Blackman Carr, Ph.D., RD, Department of Nutritional Sciences, University of Connecticut, Storrs, Connecticut. "Recruitment materials should reflect people's lived experiences, and researchers should consider the trusted community spaces and digital platforms people use in their daily lives. Just as importantly, nutrition professionals must understand the cultural and social contexts that shape food choices to help participants make meaningful changes to their health."

Participants identified both digital platforms, such as social media and YouTube, and trusted community spaces, including churches, as valuable places to share recruitment materials. Preferences varied somewhat by sex: women placed greater emphasis on traditional community settings, while men prioritized digital platforms.

These findings suggest that combining culturally relevant messaging with recruitment through familiar community spaces and digital channels may help researchers better engage Black adults, resulting in their greater representation in nutrition research.

item.description:
