Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

Navi Mumbai Cyber Police say a Rs 1.98 crore fintech intrusion ran from Hong Kong through VPN nodes hosted in a Chennai home. A second case at a digital bank and a push by banks against pre-authorised payouts show how exposed payment plumbing has become.

What happened

Navi Mumbai Cyber Police have arrested an electrical and electronics engineer in Chennai in a case where about Rs 1.98 crore was diverted from a fintech company by breaking into its server and manipulating its payment gateway, according to a Free Press Journal report updated on 25 November. Police say the intrusion was carried out from Hong Kong. The attackers reached the company's electronic ledger and its bank-linked payment gateway without valid credentials and pushed money into several bank accounts. The FIR was registered at Navi Mumbai Cyber Police Station in October 2026 and the arrest was made on 18 November.

The arrested man is not accused of writing the attack. Police allege he set up VPN nodes at his home and made them available to associates abroad, and that he was paid in cryptocurrency and through other digital channels. Investigators traced him through IP addresses linked to the bank transactions, email IDs and account details. They seized a laptop, a router, a Raspberry Pi single-board computer, a memory card and a phone, and say more than Rs 1 crore has been frozen in various accounts. The fintech company has not been named.

A separate case from the same city shows the pattern is wider. FPJ reported on 24 November that between 10 and 15 November about Rs 1.74 crore was moved out of 215 customers' accounts at a Navi Mumbai-headquartered digital payments bank, using what police called a technical loophole in one of its mobile applications. The money went into 322 internal accounts and Rs 1.56 crore was then sent to other banks in 523 transactions. The bank's anti-fraud unit flagged it on 14 November, its information security team traced two IP addresses, and it refunded all 215 customers on 17 November. The bank filed complaints on the National Cybercrime Reporting Portal on 20 November and with police on 21 November, invoking Sections 318(4), 61(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita along with IT Act provisions. It also informed RBI, CERT-In, MHA and RBI's DAKSH portal. No arrest had been reported in that case. We covered it in one paragraph in this morning's India Cyber Brief.

Why this matters now

These cases land in a month when regulators and banks are openly worried about machine-to-machine payment channels. On 4 November I4C's threat analytics unit and CERT-In issued a joint advisory warning that financially motivated attackers, using AI agents, were compromising disbursement systems and payment APIs at banks, NBFCs and fintechs, and moving multi-crore sums through mule accounts over IMPS and NEFT before deleting logs, PSU Watch reported. MediaNama reported that RBI followed with a confidential advisory asking banks to keep an inventory of API clients, whitelist beneficiaries, add maker-checker or out-of-band approval for API debits and set per-transaction and daily limits.

On 25 November Elets BFSI, citing The Economic Times, reported that banks have asked I4C and RBI to curb "pre-authorisation" arrangements, under which an NBFC's own system pushes payment instructions into bank rails and the bank pays out in bulk without a login or OTP. Bankers fear that an attacker inside an NBFC could create fake loans to mule accounts or change a genuine borrower's bank details.

Analysis: The Navi Mumbai arrest is useful because it shows the human layer behind a "foreign" intrusion. Operators abroad need Indian-looking network exits so that their traffic passes IP allow-lists and fraud scoring. A home internet connection with a small always-on device is enough to provide that, and the person renting it out becomes the traceable link, much as mule account holders are for the money.

How the scheme works

- Access. Attackers reach a server, a test environment or an exposed API at a payment company. Police in this case describe access to the ledger and payment gateway without valid credentials; the advisory reported by PSU Watch lists unpatched software and misconfigured internet-facing servers as common entry points.

- Disguise. Traffic is routed through VPN nodes, including, police allege, one run from a residence in Chennai, so that requests look domestic.

- Manipulation. Ledger entries or payout instructions are altered so the gateway sends money to new beneficiaries.

- Dispersal. Funds are split across many bank accounts and moved on quickly. In the digital bank case, 523 outward transactions followed transfers into 322 internal accounts.

- Cash-out. Helpers are paid in cryptocurrency or other digital channels, which slows the money trail.

Red flags

What to do

For ordinary users

- If you see an unexplained debit, call your bank immediately and report it on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in. Speed decides how much can be frozen.

- Do not accept money to host devices, VPNs or proxies at home for people you do not know. Police in this case traced the network exit back to the person who ran it.

- Never rent out a bank account, SIM or UPI ID. Unknown money that lands in your account should be reported in writing to your bank, not withdrawn.

- Check your bank statement and app notifications regularly; refunds in the digital bank case followed fast internal detection.

For investigators and fraud teams

- Report incidents to CERT-In within six hours of detection and, for regulated entities, on RBI's DAKSH portal, as the joint advisory asks.

- Preserve server, gateway, ledger and cloud logs before anyone "cleans up". Seek them, along with VPN provider and ISP subscriber records, through notices under Section 94 BNSS.…

item.title: Your Predictive AI Saw the Failure Coming. Nobody Changed Anything.
item.description:

Why it is here: useful vocabulary, clear explanation

Why accurate predictions are not enough, and how to turn predictive intelligence into real operational decisions

There is something strange about building an AI system that can predict a machine failure three days before it happens, only to watch that machine break down anyway.

The model did what it was designed to do. It analysed sensor readings, identified an unusual pattern, calculated a risk score and generated an alert. From a machine learning perspective, that might look like a successful outcome.

But from the perspective of a manufacturing business, the result is very different.

Production stopped. Orders were delayed. Maintenance teams were called in unexpectedly. Spare parts had to be arranged urgently. The company lost valuable production hours, and someone eventually asked a question that the AI dashboard could not answer.

If the system knew this was coming, why didn't we prevent it?

I think this is one of the most important problems facing predictive AI today. We have become increasingly good at building models that identify patterns, estimate probabilities and forecast possible outcomes. But predicting an event and changing the conditions that lead to that event are two very different engineering problems.

In manufacturing, the difference can be expensive. A predictive maintenance model might identify a 90% probability of equipment failure within the next 72 hours. That sounds impressive. But what happens next? Does a maintenance ticket get created? Does someone verify the prediction? Is the required replacement part available? Can production be rescheduled? Does a human need to approve shutting down an expensive machine?

If none of these things happens, the prediction remains an observation. And observations do not repair machines. In my view, the next important step in enterprise AI is not simply building models that predict more accurately. It is building intelligent systems that can translate predictions into decisions, coordinate the required actions and verify whether those actions actually changed the outcome.

That is where predictive intelligence becomes operational intelligence.

The difference between predicting a problem and preventing it

Let's consider a manufacturing facility operating several industrial machines across multiple production lines.

One of its critical machines contains vibration sensors, temperature sensors and pressure monitoring equipment. These sensors continuously generate information about operating conditions. The data is collected and analysed by a predictive AI system.

For several weeks, the machine has operated normally. Then the model begins identifying a combination of unusual patterns. Vibration levels are gradually increasing, operating temperature is slightly above its normal range, and pressure readings are becoming less stable.

Individually, none of these signals necessarily indicates an immediate failure. Together, however, they may indicate a developing mechanical problem. The model calculates a high risk of equipment failure within the next 72 hours. Consider the following illustrative prediction:

The prediction is useful. It allows the maintenance team to investigate before the equipment fails. However, the prediction itself does not answer several operational questions.

Is the machine actually experiencing a mechanical defect, or is the sensor producing unreliable readings? Is a technician available? Is the replacement component in stock? Can production temporarily move to another machine? Will stopping the equipment now create a larger operational problem than continuing to run it?

These questions cannot be answered by a failure probability alone. This is where many predictive AI implementations encounter difficulties. The model produces an output, but the organisation has not built the decision-making process required to act on it.

The prediction reaches a dashboard. Someone receives an email. A notification appears in a monitoring system, and then nothing happens.

The missing component is not necessarily a better machine learning algorithm. It is the operational decision layer connecting intelligence to execution.

Why accurate predictions still fail in the real world

When a predictive AI project does not deliver the expected business outcome, it is tempting to immediately question the model's accuracy.

Sometimes that is justified. Models can generate false positives, miss developing faults or perform poorly when operating conditions change. But not every failed prediction-to-action workflow is a modelling problem.

There are several other reasons why an organisation can have a technically successful predictive system and still experience preventable failures.

1. Predictions arrive, but nobody owns the decision

One of the most overlooked problems is ownership. An AI system generates an alert and sends it to a maintenance dashboard. The maintenance team assumes the production supervisor will review it. The supervisor expects the maintenance manager to approve the intervention. The maintenance manager is waiting for a technical assessment.

Everyone knows about the prediction, but nobody owns the next decision. This is an organisational problem disguised as a technology problem.

Every actionable prediction needs a defined owner. That does not mean the AI should independently decide everything. It means the system should know who is responsible for reviewing the recommendation, who can approve an intervention and what should happen if nobody responds within the required timeframe.

A prediction without an assigned decision owner is simply another notification competing for attention.

2. The model predicts risk, not operational feasibility

A model might predict that a machine has a 90% probability of failure within three days. It does not automatically know whether the factory can afford to stop that machine immediately.…

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Mock Service Worker, the API mocking library maintained by Artem Zakharchenko, has released version 3.0, nearly three years after the Fetch-based v2.0 rewrite. The release ships as ESM-only, completes the library's GraphQL story with subscription support, and introduces a socket-based interception algorithm in Node.js that Zakharchenko describes as going as deep into the runtime as JavaScript will allow without recompiling Node.

The headline breaking change is that MSW is now distributed natively as ECMAScript Modules only, with support for Node.js v18 and v20 dropped in favour of v22, v24, and v26. TypeScript 5.9 is now the minimum supported version. Several transitive dependencies have been removed, including graphql (now a proper optional peer), path-to-regexp, picocolors, and statuses. The result is a library tarball that drops from 416KB to 234KB, with type definitions shrinking by half, from 190KB to 90KB.

Alongside ESM, v3.0 introduces granular entrypoints that replace the single msw import with designated paths for each protocol:

import { http } from 'msw/http'

import { graphql } from 'msw/graphql'

import { sse } from 'msw/sse'

import { ws } from 'msw/ws'

GraphQL subscription support, a long-standing community request on the project's tracker, lands in this release. Building on the WebSocket interception shipped previously, subscription handlers can now be defined against a graphql.link() and publish events on demand, closing the gap between MSW's HTTP, WebSocket, and GraphQL coverage.

An experimental defineNetwork API is introduced as the eventual replacement for setupServer and setupWorker. The new primitive splits interception into sources (where traffic comes from) and handlers (how it is answered), allowing teams to replay HAR files, combine custom interceptors, or hand control of request timing to a test runner. The first ecosystem package to expose it directly is @msw/cloudflare, which wraps the API for Workers environments.

The most technically significant change sits in the underlying Interceptors library. Zakharchenko writes that after seven attempts at the problem, the team has moved network interception in Node.js down to the TCP and TLS wraps, the JavaScript bindings for Node's C-level network code. Moving any lower, he notes, would require recompiling Node.js itself. The new architecture supports arbitrary socket-based protocols, with SMTP cited as an early example. Nock already relies on the Interceptors library for its Node.js support.

A GitHub discussion reports failing tests after upgrading, traced to MSW now intercepting the browser-issued OPTIONS preflight requests that previous versions quietly ignored. Separately, a developer in discussion #2771 challenged the earlier decision to deprioritise Jest and JSDOM, arguing that a runner with 46 million weekly downloads warrants a formal breaking-change note rather than a quiet docs change.

In the Node-only space, MSW continues to compete with Nock, fetch-mock, and undici's built-in MockAgent, though as a recent comparison notes, none of those cover both browser and server with a single handler definition.

Teams on v2 should consult the official 2.x to 3.x migration guide before upgrading. Full release notes are available on GitHub.

Mock Service Worker is an open-source, MIT-licensed JavaScript library for mocking network traffic using Service Workers in the browser and runtime-level interception in Node.js. It is used widely for frontend and full-stack testing, and now covers HTTP, WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and GraphQL including subscriptions.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite. This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.

Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck.

sqlite3_rsync can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!

It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:

The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

17. Lions' Commentary on Unix

Lions' Commentary on Unix

John Lions was teaching operating systems at the University of New South Wales in Australia.

What's the best way to

teach operating systems?

They need to study the Unix source.

But it's tough going.

I'll write my

own textbook.

In May 1976, Lions prepared lecture notes explaining the kernel source code of AT&T's Unix Version 6. These became his Unix commentary.

To understand an OS,

we need to read

the actual code.

I've written a guide

to the Unix kernel.

We'll use it as

our textbook.

By 1977, the notes were circulating among other schools and research institutions with Unix licenses [1][4]. Even Bell Labs wanted copies and eventually took over distribution [2].

Early on, Unix source could be studied in class. But at USENIX in June 1979, AT&T announced new Version 7 license terms restricting courses that disclosed or discussed source code. Distribution of Lions' book was tightly controlled as well [5][6].

I am altering the license.

Pray I don't alter it

any further.

Destroy Lions' book.

No more teaching

Unix source code.

There is no escape

from our operating system.

He's teaching from the Unix source code!

Seize the books!

Run!

He's got the book!

Don't let him

escape!

Quick! Take

the book!

Ugh!

I find your interest

in source code disturbing.

Just use the system calls.

Learn a little theory.

Leave the internals to us.

Theory isn't enough.

I need to see the code.

This code is our only hope

of understanding an OS.

For roughly twenty years before the official edition appeared, computer-science students studied from unauthorized photocopies. The book helped a generation of students learn to build operating systems of their own [5][8].

Meanwhile, members of the Unix community, including Peter H. Salus, Dennis Ritchie and Berny Goodheart, kept asking AT&T, Novell and the Santa Cruz Operation for permission to publish the book. SCO finally agreed. Peer-to-Peer Communications published the official edition in 1996 [5][7].

Lions' book is finally

in print. It even has

my foreword.

People were secretly copying it

for twenty years?

Unbelievable.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.

The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.

Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.

Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the new core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.

A Faster Frontend

Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.

Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.

High core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.…

Semiconductors are surpassing oil as the linchpin of the dollar’s global reach, demonstrating U.S. technological might but also revealing a less stable foundation, according to Deutsche Bank.

In a note last week, foreign exchange strategist Mallika Sachdeva pointed out that for the first time in modern history, global trade in chips now exceeds trade in oil and gas. Excluding China, Asia’s surplus in the chip trade matches petroleum-related surpluses in the Persian Gulf, she added.

That’s as AI hyperscalers keep ramping up capital expenditures, which are expected to top $1 trillion next year, further propping up chip trade flows.

“The rise of chips as a driver of dollar dominance can be seen as a symptom of change in the ultimate source of U.S. power — from geopolitical to technological leadership,” Sachdeva wrote, adding that the so-called petrodollar is quickly being superseded by the new “chip-dollar.”

The petrodollar regime goes back to a deal struck in 1974 when Saudi Arabia agreed to price its oil in dollars and invest surpluses in U.S. assets, especially Treasury debt. In return, the American military ensured security in the region and free navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

And because oil is a core input to global manufacturing and transport, supply chains have a natural incentive to dollarize. Indeed, Mideast oil and gas are used to make petrochemicals, fertilizer, and even helium.

But the underpinnings of the petrodollar are breaking down due to the Iran war as Tehran exposes the limits of the U.S. military, while the AI boom is sending a tsunami of capital from Asia to the U.S.

This time around, rather than Mideast kingdoms recycling oil-trade surpluses into U.S. debt, Asia’s chip behemoths are recycling chip-trade surpluses into U.S. stocks. In fact, South Korean households have 90% of their equity exposure in the U.S., according to Deutsche Bank. Overall, foreign purchases of U.S. equities are now more than double that of Treasuries.

“The emerging chip-dollar regime is one where US technology leadership is motivating global savings to be reinvested in U.S. companies — providing funding for the US corporate sector to make enormous investments in new technology such as AI,” Sachdeva explained.

Chip dominance begets dollar dominance

Just like how oil penetrated industrial supply chain, chips are embedded in the digital economy as inputs in consumer electronics, automobiles, computers, communication devices, and AI systems. She estimated chips account for more than 50% of the capex for a data center.

And despite Asia’s dominance in chipmaking, 70% of the industry’s profits flow to U.S. firms. In addition, the key countries in the supply chain of advanced chips are friendly with Washington, namely Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

“The potent combination of U.S. control over key upstream technologies and intellectual property, alongside a supply chain located in U.S. allies has given the U.S. enormous control over chips,” Sachdeva added.

At the same time, chips ensure continued dollar dominance in global trade, payments, capital markets, and private sector savings, while also supporting America’s AI buildout, she pointed out.

But Deutsche Bank cautioned that the new currency regime has a “circularity” risk because capital flowing from Asian chip hotspots provides financing to U.S. companies driving the AI boom. That means if consumer demand for compute can’t support AI investments, earnings for tech companies would come down—as well as chip demand.

The focus on stocks over debt means more instability too. U.S. stocks overall are three times as volatile as Treasuries—and tech stocks are up to 10 times as much, Sachdeva noted.

“A dollar driven by chips, AI and private capital connections should be inherently riskier,” she warned.

That risk was on display in recent weeks as tech stocks sold off sharply on fears the AI boom was about to go bust. And although Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia on Monday sparked a big rebound, the Trump administration is cracking down on foreign access to U.S. AI technology, potentially curbing the chip trade.

Dollar vs. yuan — Coke vs. Pepsi

To be sure, threats to the dollar’s status as the global reserve currency have come and gone over the decades. More recently, the proliferation of U.S. financial sanctions has given countries more reason to diversify away from the dollar.

But no credible alternatives have emerged yet, despite China’s aggressive efforts to internationalize the yuan.

China facilitates its use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets. Beijing also promotes “China prices,” or yuan benchmarks on domestic commodity exchanges. Chinese banks have more than doubled their yuan lending to overseas borrowers since 2023, and the central bank has reached currency swap agreements with dozens of peers.

But Zongyuan Zoe Liu, senior fellow for China studies at the Council on Foreign Relation, argued in Foreign Affairs last month that Beijing doesn’t actually want to replace the dollar on the world stage.

“Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy,” she wrote.

“From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.”

Millions of Americans, and their financial futures, may be exposed to the recent AI-fueled swings in the market regardless of whether they’ve ever used a chatbot.

Stocks plunged Wednesday morning before recovering much of the loss. Near the start of trading, the Dow fell more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% as AI chip stocks sold off for a second straight day. Nvidia fell as much as 8%. By late afternoon, the S&P 500 had cut its loss to about half a percent, and the Dow had turned higher.

Wednesday’s swing capped a week in which a single company’s board decision moved the index that holds much of Americans’ retirement accounts. Roughly two-thirds of of Fidelity 401(k) savers keep everything in a target-date fund.

Following a tumultuous few weeks in which Jensen Huang resigned and was later reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, the chipmaker’s stock jumped 31%, added about $950 billion in market value, and lifted the S&P 500 by 4.7%. Still, the S&P 500 is now about 8% below its Oct. 6 record. Last Friday it closed 11.6% below that high, putting it in correction territory, after seven straight losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Stock market concentration has been on the rise for years, and it is now near 35-year highs. Just 10 stocks in the S&P 500 account for about 39% of its total market capitalization, with the five largest stocks—all tech giants—alone accounting for 29%, according to Charles Schwab. That means an American with $100,000 in an index fund tied to the S&P 500 would have $29,000 in just five stocks.

As a result, many investors may think they are putting money into a diversified investment when the health of their portfolios may actually be tied more to the fate of a handful of tech giants than they realize, said Martin Mulyadi, a professor of accounting at Shenandoah University’s College of Business, Engineering & Technology.

“An index fund spreads your money across 500 companies, but it does not spread the risk evenly,” he told Fortune.

For the millions of Americans who have poured their money into S&P 500 index funds through their 401(k)s, this concentration has been a boon in recent years. A booming stock market that has risen just over 50% during the past five years helped push the number of 401(k) millionaires at Fidelity to a record 769,000 in June. Even before the selloff began, that number had fallen some 2% between the second and third quarters, but was still up 15% from a year earlier, according to Fidelity.

Through the third quarter, the vast majority of retirement savers were still investing. About 96% of 401(k) participants at Fidelity either maintained or increased their savings rate during the third quarter, the financial services company revealed in a report this week.

“Despite market volatility, many workers continue to increase their savings, stay invested, and take advantage of workplace retirement plan features designed to support long-term success,” Sharon Brovelli, Fidelity’s president of workplace investing, said in a statement.

Yet the growing dominance of a handful of technology giants means even those who have followed conventional retirement wisdom and have added to diversified funds may be exposed to heightened risk.

A further stock slide could hurt the portfolios of millions of Americans and especially for those closer to retirement: The average Fidelity 401(k) millionaire is 58 years old.

Retirement at risk

For older Americans, a downturn early in retirement could have implications for when they can afford to stop working and how much money they’ll have to live on once they do.

By selling investments at depressed prices to cover living expenses, retirees face the problem of sequence-of-returns risk. If a falling stock market in early retirement causes retirees to sell their investments at lower prices, that means they have less money left in the market that could later benefit from an eventual recovery.

To try to avoid this phenomenon, Charles Schwab recommends maintaining a short-term reserve of low-risk and more liquid investments that retirees could draw from in a downturn to avoid touching their portfolio.

The increasing concentration of the stock market also doesn’t necessarily mean investors should abandon index funds altogether. Investors should instead consider taking a closer look at the makeup of their portfolio, said Sean McEvilly, the managing partner and founder of Vistamark Investments.

“The practical move isn’t to bail out of stocks. It’s to look at the whole 401(k), since target-date and large-cap funds often hold the same names, and make sure there’s real exposure to small and midsized companies, international stocks, and bonds,” McEvilly told Fortune.

In a time of rising costs, one Thanksgiving commodity is cheaper: cannabis

This Thanksgiving season, Americans are paying more for almost everything: travel costs have soared, and the price of food has risen. Bringing wine to the family dinner? That costs more, too.

But there's one thing consumers buy at high rates that will actually get cheaper this time of year: marijuana.

Known in the industry as "Green Week" or "Green Wednesday," the days ahead of Thanksgiving have come to rival famed stoner holiday 4/20 as the day cannabis dispensaries see the most sales — and highest foot traffic — of the year.

In most dispensaries around the country, that means steep discounts, doorbuster specials and exclusive products. It's a good deal for customers, who line up in long queues as they await their turn with the so-called budtenders behind the counter.

Cannabis in the U.S. is a $30 billion industry with legal marketplaces in 24 states and the nation's capital, according to Whitney Economics, a firm that specializes in economic research and consulting on the business of cannabis. But in recent years, the deep discounts that have drawn in customers — and kept them coming back for weeks like this one — have squeezed retailers and resulted in a revenue decline in the legal market.

As the week began at The Forest, a dispensary in Baltimore, shoppers were stocking up for the holiday week.

A pack of gummies to bring to Friendsgiving in lieu of alcohol. A sparkling THC-infused beverage for those canna-curious in-laws. Or a holiday staple: some pre-rolls to share on an evening walk.

On bright screens posted around the store, discount offers flashed: 25% off edibles, read one; 30% off for medical patients, read another. An extra $5 off for bringing in cans of food for the store's holiday drive.

Kelley Vinton, 36, is a regular at The Forest. She's a medical marijuana user and usually sticks to a strict weekly budget, she said. But on Monday, she threw in a few little extras — for the "cousin walk," Vinton said.

"You know, you take a little breaky-poo with your cousins, and we live in the country, so we just walk, usually before dinner," Vinton said. "We smoke a joint, and we get nice and high, and get some munchies and get ready for dinner."

The federal government still classifies recreational marijuana as a Schedule I drug, meaning it is considered to have "high potential for abuse," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration. But medical cannabis was reclassified this year to Schedule III, a category shared by drugs like Tylenol with codeine and anabolic steroids.

In 2025, Whitney Economics found, revenue was down across the industry thanks to an oversupply of plant product and declining prices, driven by the discount culture of cannabis retailers.

It was the first year since 2014 — when Colorado and Washington became the first states to legalize cannabis sales for recreational use — that the industry saw a dip, according to an analysis by Whitney Economics.

"It's forced a race to the bottom," said Beau Whitney, the founder and chief economist at Whitney Economics. "What this is resulting in is great prices for the consumer, they're spending less and getting the same or more, so that's good for them on an affordability perspective. But it's hurting operators."

Though the industry has seen a slight rebound this year — an increase of about 5% in sales for the same period last year, Whitney's team found — forecasts for the end of 2026 and the outlook for 2027 remain relatively modest.

The biggest reason for this, Whitney said, is customer behavior.

Through the beginning of the 2020s, Whitney said, consumers would typically come into a dispensary with a set amount to spend. Their cannabis budget. If they got a discount, Whitney said, they'd add additional products into their carts to hit their budget.

But that began to change in 2024, as inflation rose and the cost of essentials, like gas, ballooned.

"Behavior changed literally overnight," Whitney said. "What they're doing is they're taking the discounts — and there's a lot of them now — and they're using that money to buy gas and buy groceries. So they're adjusting the amount that they purchase based on what's going on in their own personal economy."

The discount model, he said, has also forced prices down. With legal retailers competing for a pool of customers that has not seen rapid growth in years, discounts help draw people into stores. But they've also created a culture where customers expect them, several cannabis store owners said.

It's why doing well on a week like this one, as customers flood in for Green Wednesday deals, is essential for shop owners like The Forest's Christina Betancourt Johnson.

On Monday, the Baltimore store was stocked — with edibles and pre-rolls and other cannabis products, but also stacks of snacks for customers waiting in longer-than-usual lines, branded giveaways and samples of gummies to try (no weed in those).

A steady flow of customers wandered in. Some for their usual supplies, others for a little holiday shopping.

Employee Thomas Bourne loaded a vape into a paper bag for one of the dispensary's regular customers. That seemed a little light for the holiday, he observed, teasingly.

"Gotta come back for your cousin walk essentials, man," Bourne said. "'Tis the week."

The customer smiled, nodding. He'd be back.

item.description:

- In Malaysia’s Terengganu state, former turtle egg collectors now work to protect a critically endangered river terrapin as part of a program led by the Turtle Conservation Society of Malaysia.

- Since the program began in 2011, the program’s “Terrapin Guardians” have collected and incubated more than 13,000 eggs and released more than 8,200 young terrapins back into the river.

- In addition to egg gathering for consumption, Terengganu’s river terrapins are also threatened by natural predators like monitor lizards and sand mining, which destroys the sandbanks the turtles nest in.

KEMAMAN, Malaysia — As night settles over Kampung Pasir Gajah, a small team of men can be found sitting in the moonlight by the riverbank. They scroll on their phones, share a late meal, but their ears are tuned to the river.

These men call themselves the Terrapin Guardians, or Geng Tuntung in Malay, after tuntung, the local word for river turtles. During nesting season from January to March, they work nights from 10 p.m. until dawn along this stretch of river in Terengganu state, on the east coast of Peninsular Malaysia. They scan for tracks of a heavy shell on the sand — a sign that a southern river terrapin (Batagur affinis) has crawled out of the water to nest.

Samsul bin Hamid, 52, a factory production line worker, was once among the villagers who gathered by these riverbanks to harvest terrapin eggs as a seasonal delicacy. He stopped after learning more about the species through the Turtle Conservation Society of Malaysia (TCS).

“I learned the ways to track terrapins through friends. Back then, they would invite me to go egg collecting, and I would go. It’s just something we learned being part of the village,” he says.

Today, Samsul is one of 13 guardians, all of whom once harvested eggs and now work with TCS to secure nests before natural threats and other collectors find them. According to TCS data, the guardians have collected and incubated 13,224 eggs, and successfully released more than 8,200 young terrapins back into the river since the community-led conservation program began in 2011.

The southern river terrapin is listed as critically endangered on the IUCN Red List, meaning the species faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild. Once widespread across Southeast Asian river basins, much of its remaining wild population is found here in Peninsular Malaysia.

In 2010, all freshwater turtles and tortoises were declared fully protected species under Malaysia’s Wildlife Conservation Act.

Eggs were about traditions, not trade

Unlike wildlife trade driven by lucrative profits, terrapin eggs collected in Kampung Pasir Gajah were traditionally shared among neighbors and eaten at home. It’s a seasonal tradition — part of village life here, Samsul explains: “The villagers collect these eggs for their own consumption, we don’t sell them.”

Even if the villagers wanted to commercialize their harvest, the monetary incentive is slim. Chen Pelf Nyok, co-founder and executive director of TCS and affectionately known as the “mother of terrapins,” says that a typical clutch of 35 eggs could be shared among as many as 10 people.

“Each person would receive only three to four eggs. Even if they sold those eggs at 8-10 ringgit [$2-$2.5] each, they would only earn around 24-40 ringgit [$6-$10],” she says. “This is very different from commercial sea turtle egg trading, where a trader could potentially earn 350-500 ringgit [$86-$123] from a single clutch of green turtle eggs.”

Still, the change didn’t come easily. “It takes a lot of patience, relationship-building and mutual respect. We engage with local communities, explain why collecting and eating terrapin eggs is illegal in Malaysia, and encourage people to become part of the conservation solution rather than simply telling them to stop,” Pelf says.

Not everyone has stopped. Some villagers still wait by the riverbank to collect eggs for their own consumption. “There were some in the village that couldn’t accept us not eating the eggs anymore,” Samsul says. “But over time, more villagers grew curious about why the terrapins needed protecting.”

Samsul also frames the work in terms of his Muslim faith. “We have a role in protecting the terrapins. Caring for animals is a virtuous act in the eyes of religion,” he said.

A terrapin guardian’s day at work

When a guardian spots a nesting terrapin, they monitor and wait for the mother to nest. Then, the team weighs, measures, and microchips the female before securing her eggs. These eggs are brought back to the TCS hatchery, incubated for three months, and the hatchlings nursed until they’re ready to be released back into the wild.

Mohd Azriezal bin Mahad, 29, is a second-generation guardian. His late father, Pak Wazel, worked with TCS from the start in 2011, and Azriezal began observing at a young age what his father was doing before officially joining this year. He’s shy and a man of few words.

When asked how he feels about working with TCS, his response is simple. “I feel happy to continue my dad’s work,” he says in a quiet voice.

The guardians are also expanding their help to the wildlife department, lending their expertise in tracking and catching river terrapins in other parts of Malaysia.

Experts say the success of a community-based conservation project isn’t dependent on the number of hatchlings released, but whether changes in human behavior last.

“The most important contribution of community-based programs is their social impact,” Natalia Gallego-García of the Tortoise and Freshwater Turtle Specialist Group at the IUCN, the global wildlife conservation authority, says in an email. Referring to conservation programs in general, she says that, “They transform how local communities perceive and value a species, creating opportunities for education and fostering a deep sense of ownership.”

Brazil has taken a step toward formally recognizing the Indigenous land where one of the Amazon rainforest’s best-known defenders, Indigenous leader Raoni Metuktire, was born.

The Mẽbêngôkre, or Kayapó, and Yudjá, or Juruna, peoples live on the 362,000-hectare (895,000-acre) Kapôt Nhĩnore Indigenous Territory, on the border between Pará and Mato Grosso states in the southern Brazilian Amazon. They have been fighting for legal rights to their land since 2004.

On Nov. 19, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, announced in a ceremony a government order that recognizes the two peoples’ permanent right to the territory. For full legal recognition, the territory still needs its borders marked on the ground, final approval by presidential decree and official registration. Only then can authorities remove non-Indigenous occupants.

About 83% of the territory still has its original forest, according to data from Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency, Funai, but has been gradually occupied by cattle ranchers and soy farmers. Deforestation increased dramatically from 4,178 hectares (10,300 acres) in 2000 to 58,000 hectares (143,300 acres) by 2026.

According to Sumaúma, an Amazon-based publication, eight large cattle ranches in the territory sell directly or indirectly to the international meat-processing company JBS. Sumaúma also identified 14 properties growing soy.

If the territory is left unprotected, such agricultural developments could multiply. A recent Greenpeace Brasil report suggests 259 registered farms and ranches overlapping 95.6% of the Indigenous territory as of February 2026. The registration with Brazil’s rural land registry, known as CAR, is reported by landholders and does not guarantee a land title, ownership of the land, or mean that forest has been destroyed.

To protect other Indigenous lands still awaiting full recognition, Greenpeace Brasil has pushed Brazil’s National Monetary Council, which sets rural credit rules, to bar farms that overlap these lands from rural credit.

“Any overlap of farms with Indigenous lands delimited, declared or placed under restriction by Funai must be grounds for denying rural credit,” Cristiane Mazzetti, coordinator of Greenpeace Brasil’s Zero Deforestation campaign, said in a statement.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value, and diversity

- Working elephants in Nepal allow crucial access to hazardous terrain for organizations like the National Trust for Nature Conservation to manage wildlife populations.

- The practice of using trained elephants is controversial and poses safety risks to both the elephants and the mahouts who work with them.

- Nepal’s working elephant populations are maintained through a breeding center near Chitwan National Park, but there’s a risk of population decline due to factors such as disease.

- New conservation techniques like genetic ID-based monitoring may come to rival the direct, elephant-borne approach for work such as the five-yearly rhino census.

CHITWAN NATIONAL PARK, Nepal — Perched some 3 meters off the ground, or about 10 feet, on the back of Asian elephants, workers traverse Nepal’s dense jungles and grasslands to complete wildlife counts, rescue distressed animals, and manage wildlife such as tigers (Panthera tigris) and greater one-horned rhinos (Rhinoceros unicornis).

Working elephants have long played an important role in the conservation of Nepal’s wildlife and wildlands. Their height and sharp sense of their surroundings keep researchers safe from tigers and other predators, and they’re also used on patrols. But dwindling captive elephant populations and opposition to using the highly intelligent animals as beasts of burden are changing the long-term outlook for working elephants and the men known as mahouts who work with them.

Dr. Amir Sadaula works closely with elephants and mahouts as a veterinary officer at the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), which operates a biodiversity conservation center on the edge of Chitwan National Park. There, NTNC employs eight trained elephants and teams of mahouts to aid in wild animal rescue and research work.

“Without [the] elephant, we could not do the rescue,” Sadaula says.

In addition to elephants that aid researchers, privately owned elephants also walk the streets of Sauraha, a community adjacent to Chitwan. Tourism companies in the gateway community often own one or two elephants and offer elephant rides to tourists as a way to experience wildlife up close. Captive elephants around Chitwan typically work with one to three mahouts.

Nepal’s Elephant Conservation Action Plan (2025-2035) recognizes the importance of maintaining the captive elephant population. It also acknowledges that elephants are vulnerable to diseases like tuberculosis and elephant endotheliotropic herpes virus, and that their treatment is dependent on limited funding and resources.

“Captive elephants in Nepal do not appear to have a future in itself unless strategic management intervention is made,” the plan says. “Captive and trained elephant population is crucial for the management of Tarai national parks and wildlife reserves and for special works such as wildlife population monitoring, rescue and translocations, and patrolling.” The Tarai, or Terai Arc, is the lowland expanse that straddles southern Nepal and part of India, where iconic species like tigers and rhinos roam.

In the field

On a typical day, a couple of mahouts will take an elephant to harvest bundles of tall grass at the crack of dawn. Back at the stables, others bundle the grass with grain to feed the elephants. This structure can be hierarchical: senior mahouts ride while others work bundling food and cleaning stalls.

Mahouts eat and change into fresh clothing before the bulk of their day’s work begins around 9:30 a.m. They heat water over a fire and sharpen sickles on a wet block. When they’re ready, they unchain the elephants, and command them to kneel on the grass, ready to accept a rider.

The first and last stop of their day is in a river to bathe. The mahouts perch barefoot on the back of their elephant, balancing to avoid the water. At their command, the elephants roll and shower in the swirling stream. Clean and satisfied, the elephants exit the river and walk into the brush, grazing on the banks of tall grass until the late afternoon.

During conservation work, the elephants’ days are busy.

The NTNC facilitates a rhino census every five years across the country’s rhino habitat. The last was in 2021, employing 57 elephants and 350 people, 250 of whom conducted a count across of Chitwan National Park, according to the 2021 report by the NTNC. The next census was due this year, but has been pushed back to next year over budget delays.

From the back of the elephants, census takers can look down and across the tall grasses to directly observe individual rhinos — something they wouldn’t be able to do if they were walking on the ground or driving in a jeep.

Researchers say they prefer the direct observation method of counting rhinos, describing it as more accurate and effective. However, new technologies make it possible to determine the population size without actually laying eyes on each individual animal.

ID-based monitoring uses field observations to create a genetic profile for each animal and allows the count to be made by analyzing dung samples or distinct markings.

During direct observation, the elephant-borne census teams sweep through the forest until each rhino is found, recorded, and allowed to pass through their phalanx. This practice, according to researchers, mitigates the risk of inaccurate data.

To ensure the reliability of the data, the process is intense. The elephants and staff may encounter the park’s wild elephants, such as Dhurbe, an adult bull notorious for aggressive encounters with humans. Dhurbe attacked and injured several census workers in 2021. Tigers, too, can pose a threat: one killed a mahout during the 2021 census in Bardia National Park, northwest of Chitwan.

“We can’t go near elephants or tigers without elephants,” says Harindra Chaudhary, a mahout for more than three decades. “We can only dart an animal if it is within 30-foot [9-m] range only.” He adds this is important as the national parks don’t have much in the way of drivable roads.…

The U.S. Army detonated five tons of degraded lead azide explosives in southeast Iowa this morning, following delays and legal challenges over concerns about toxic dust generated by the blast.

Cars passed along the north end of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown a minute before the detonation, with more traffic passing soon afterward.

At an 11 a.m. briefing, Army officials also said initial air monitoring had detected no airborne lead.

Measuring airborne lead is more complicated than a single reading might suggest, said Bruce Lanphear, an expert on lead exposure and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. The monitoring methods used, the size of the particles being measured and the height and location of monitoring equipment can all affect the results.

“The failure to detect an increase in airborne lead from preliminary samples does not establish that no lead was released or that no one was exposed,” Lanphear said in an email exchange with Inside Climate News on Wednesday. Lanphear submitted an expert witness statement in support of an emergency lawsuit filed last week on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter.

Is It Safe to Eat from a Charcuterie Board That’s Been Out All Afternoon?

Charcuterie boards are a party favorite, but how long can they safely sit out? Here's what to know before you grab another bite of that wilted cheese.

I totally understand the excitement that comes from spying a gorgeous charcuterie board at a gathering. Between the cheeses, the cured meats and all the little finger foods, there are too many potential combinations to wonder how long everything has been sitting out. But as a registered dietitian, I can’t help thinking about it!

Food safety was a big deal in my studies, and all those lessons about safe cooking temperatures, proper food handling and food storage have stuck with me. After all, cut a few corners here or let food sit out a little too long there, and you could find yourself in a real pickle—one where you risking spoiling all that delicious food you took time to prepare.

So, how long can a charcuterie board safely sit out before it’s time to show it the bin? With the holidays in full swing and cheese boards popping up at just about every gathering, these food safety tips will keep you snacking happily and safely all season long.

Can you eat from a charcuterie board that’s been sitting out?

Yes, but you’ll want to keep an eye on the clock! Most perishable items on a charcuterie board—including soft cheeses, deli meats, chilled dips and cut fruit—shouldn’t sit at room temperature for more than two hours. If the temperature is above 90°F (like at an outdoor summer party), that window shrinks to just one hour.

Harmful bacteria can multiply quickly when perishable foods spend too much time in the temperature danger zone, which is between 40°F and 140°F. And unfortunately food doesn’t have to look or smell spoiled to be unsafe to eat.

Some charcuterie boards are designed to keep food chilled, with built-in compartments for ice packs or trays that sit over ice. If the perishable foods are kept at 40°F or below, they can stay out a little longer without entering the temperature danger zone.

One thing to keep in mind: The clock starts when the perishable foods come out of the refrigerator, not when guests start digging in. If a charcuterie board has been sitting out for more than two hours, it’s safest to toss the perishable items rather than save them for later.

And if you’re a guest and aren’t sure how long the board has been sitting out, you have a couple options. You can either casually ask the host, or you can skip the perishable items altogether and stick with shelf-stable munchies like crackers, seasoned nuts and pretzels.

Can some cheeses stay out longer than others?

Sort of! Hard cheeses like Parmesan, Manchego and aged Gouda handle room temperature better than soft cheeses like Brie, fresh goat cheese, fresh mozzarella and cream cheese.

That’s because hard cheeses contain less moisture, so they’re a little less hospitable to the harmful bacteria that can make you sick. Soft cheeses have more moisture, so they’re more perishable and should follow the same strict two-hour rule as other refrigerated foods.

While hard cheeses are a safer bet than soft varieties, that doesn’t mean they can sit out indefinitely! They’re still subject to food safety concerns, so if you’re not sure how long the board has been sitting out, it’s safest to skip the perishable items regardless of the cheese type.

Signs That a Charcuterie Board Has Been Out Too Long

You can’t always tell if food is safe to eat just by looking at it, but there are a few visible signs that a charcuterie board may have been sitting out for a while. You might notice cheeses sweating or getting extra soft or oily, or you might see sliced meats starting to look dried out around the edges. Cut fruit may also turn mushy or discolored as it sits.

Not everything on a cheese board carries the same food safety risk. When in doubt, don’t take a chance on foods that need refrigeration. You can always fill your plate with the shelf-stable nuts, crackers and whole fruit instead.

If you’re hosting, put out smaller portions of cheeses and meats and replenish the board as needed. That way, you can keep the extra food refrigerated until it’s time to serve more, rather than letting everything sit out for hours.

Jabez Bartlett channels “brutalist-folk” spirit for debut furniture collection

The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.

Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he showed a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.

A circular version followed, and both pieces are part of The Freight Proportioned to the Groove, an exhibition of his debut furniture collection that opens today in Hackney, London.

Bartlett told Dezeen that he wanted to start creating furniture to experiment with materials that he has used to bring film sets to life on screen.

“With set design, things don’t necessarily have to be practical,” said the Devon-born designer. “It’s all about how they look on camera. I wanted to play with this in a more material and physical world.”

“There’s a lot of industrial materials we’ve always used that I think are incredibly beautiful,” he continued. “It’s interesting to use something heavy and practical in a luxury piece.”

Bartlett’s collection includes a triptych of marbled dining chairs made from a mixture of microcrystalline and crude oil wax cast in plywood frames.

The pieces were informed by a Japanese games table owned by the designer, characterised by a gridded top.

“I had the idea to remake it as a giant candle, with a wick in each square,” he explained. The idea became three chunky chairs that resemble large candles, embellished with playful wicks.

Bartlett’s collection also features a trio of lighting pieces clad in stretchy latex skins.

The smallest is a ceramic table lamp with a bloated shade, while the other two are angular floor lamps supported by metal structures, one of which was on display at the southwest London gallery Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

Despite their industrial materials, Bartlett also considers his pieces as nods to the wilderness.

“I started off wanting to make brutalist-folk furniture, and now I’m seeing it, I feel like I got there,” he said. “Memory and illusion play a big part, and of course, growing up in Devon leaves an imprint of the natural and the ancient world on you.”

Another of the collection’s pieces is a large diamond-patterned textile rug, overdyed and bleached, and embellished with metal tags normally used to identify cattle.

The tags hem the rug and were also embroidered into its fabric in decorative circles.

Also on display in the exhibition are a monolithic cast acrylic mirror, a glossy black plinth and column with protruding thorns and another floor lamp with a similarly spiky, elongated black body and a sandy leather shade.

The title of Bartlett’s exhibition refers to the final line of poet Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century poem, That Love is All There Is.

The Freight Proportioned to the Groove is on display from 26 to 29 November at Tuscany Wharf, 4B Orsman Road, London N1 5QJ. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

Why it is here: original reporting, detailed design analysis

Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Why Burlwood Continues to Captivate Designers

“Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

For Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he says. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

“The material is timeless,” Brooks says. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”

Fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-new piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he says, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Choosing the Right Burlwood

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

Maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he says.

While Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she says. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”

Pairing Burlwood with Other Materials and Finishes

Because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she says. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

Meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

For a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

How Designers Are Reimagining Burlwood

Burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she says. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.…

‘Pay attention and stay curious’: Réka Matyas on her charming little worlds filled with spotty dogs and polka-dog cats

The Budapest-based illustrator fills her colourful drawings with curious characters and unexpected details, encouraging us to slow down and find joy in the everyday.

Spend a few minutes in Réka Mátyás’ portfolio, and you’ll meet two spotty dogs gazing at each other across a green meadow, a polka-dot cat posing beside an equally polka-dot tabi shoe, and a woman with ladybugs crawling through her golden hair. Polka-dot sisters, three cats stretched out across a chocolate-brown page, and a figure cradling a birthday cake with a single lit candle appear. It all feels soft, warm and slightly odd, splashed in a playful palette of bubblegum pinks, grassy greens and buttery yellows.

The Budapest-based illustrator and motion designer was born in Transylvania, Romania, and began her creative journey at university, where she studied Fine Arts and graduated with a BA in 2022. She experimented with all sorts of materials and mediums, though pencil sketches and realistic drawing were her real loves. By the end of her degree, she admits, she “felt quite lost”, with plenty of pressure to find her own style. So she took a year off and landed a role at a small creative studio as a motion designer, where she picked up the software, dabbled in graphic design, and started to see new possibilities. That led her to Budapest for a master’s in Graphic Design, which she completed in 2025. Today, she works full-time as a motion designer at Artbinary, “an amazing agency where I feel like part of the family”, while illustration fills her free time, along with the occasional graphic design project when something resonates.

For a long while, Réka felt she had to pick one path out of the three. “It stressed me out quite a bit,” she says. “But over time, I’ve learned to embrace all three, and I finally feel like I’ve found my place. I’ve also realised that switching between them keeps me creatively fresh. Each discipline gives me a different perspective and a little breathing room from the others, allowing me to return to my work with new ideas and push it in directions I might not have discovered otherwise. Now, rather than seeing these different paths as competing with each other, I see them as things that feed into and strengthen one another.”

With the world around her as her muse, Réka’s ideas usually come from everyday moments. “I’m interested in observing people, their lives and the little moments that might seem insignificant at first,” she says. Réka then jots these observations down or makes quick sketches in a notebook, where an idea might sit for months before it finds its way into an illustration. Nature, music, films and whatever book she’s reading chip in too, because “you just have to pay attention and stay curious”.

When the time comes to make something, Réka sits quietly for a few minutes and lets her mind wander, imagining a little scenario around the theme. Then comes lots of tiny, rough pencil or coloured-pen sketches. “They’re usually pretty ugly, and I almost always hate all of them at first!” she laughs, but this messy stage is where the final concept tends to appear, often somewhere completely different from where she started. Once something feels right, she plays with the composition, mood and colour, then moves to her iPad, which she says is usually the quickest part.

Among her favourites is an illustration for ZEITmagazine, commissioned by art director Viola Hasse, and her first editorial job. She had never drawn older people before, so she dived straight into sketching, starting with the couple at the centre – looking lovingly into each other’s eyes – and building a story around them with symbols and perspectives. Réka loves to build worlds in her illustrations – artworks that make people smile, ask their viewers to slow down and take in the beauty around them. And each piece comes with its own set of characters and plots, using tiny details she would have spotted in her own reality.

“I usually try to include a small, unexpected detail in my illustrations, something that might surprise people or make them look twice,” she says. “I like the idea of creating images that reveal a little more the longer you spend with them. Ultimately, I don’t think every illustration needs to carry a big message. Sometimes, making someone smile or helping them see something familiar in a slightly different way is more than enough.”

The Natural History of the Sea-Serpent

Published in Koot-Hoomi’s Quarterly, New Lovegain, 1341.

The patron who does us the honor to take up this article, as a gentle preparative for an after-dinner nap, may, perhaps, pardon us for reminding them that the soft turquoise light of their sitting-room lamp is borrowed from the largest and most ferocious of known creatures; that the oil which turns night into day, and invests its power upon the steam-engines of our manufactories and rail-roads, once formed part of a vast and fearsome being whose heart sent out twenty or thirty gallons of blood at every stroke, through an aorta measuring more than two feet in diameter; and that the creature whose gigantic frame was nourished by this flood of life gamboled on the broad back of the World-Ocean, rejoicing in its strength, till the minuscule, mortal human, whose engines had grown hungry for the wyrms’ treacly ichor, made war upon the beast in its own realm, and left the enormous mass inanimate. Nor is every one acquainted with the dangers and privations borne by those who seek the terrible monster in its remote watery demesne. A serpent-hunting voyage often exceeds three years, and hardly ever occupies less than two. From the port of New Lovegain alone an average of seventy sail of fine ships, of a burthen ranging from three to four hundred tons, are annually on the look-out for the fattest of sea-serpents. The crews of these ships, which are fully provisioned for three years, and sail from New Lovegain at all times of the year, consist of from twenty-eight to thirty-three sailors and officers—including at least one sorcerer, typically a tempestarius also serving as navigational astrologer, which, after all, seems to us to be a very commendable species of mixed practice. As, for obvious reasons, there are in such expeditions “no more cats than can catch mice,” the mariner who has been afloat in one of these ships is pretty sure to turn out a crack specimen of their genus—a smart character, case-hardened to any climate, expert in all their professional duties—endued with imperturbable nerves and quick decision, eagle-eyed, and tyger-hearted.

All the sailors are, in point of fact, co-adventurers with the owner; for they go “on the lay”—that is, they have a certain share of the produce, instead of the ordinary money-payment. This arrangement, which sailors find eminently favorable to employment in the smoky labyrinths of New Lovegain’s rail-fed manufactories, can be ascribed to the influence of the Mazuraa cultus, particularly those clades which favor the worship of the Deep Goddess in Her incarnation as Gykylyk, Mother of Storms. Such teachings have long argued that the great serpents, being ex nihilo and tempore ruinae the creation of their favored goddess, therefore exist as the common property of humankind, who have worked for over a millennium to appease the deities’ displeasure. The rewards of the serpents’ oil, the sea-laborers have proclaimed, should then at least be shared equitably amongst the crew who procured the stuff.

The zeal with which this dangerous sea-hunt is pursued seems to take the strongest possession of the sailors’ minds; and one of their most usual modes of making a heavy hour light is sketching their favorite ship, serpents in various attitudes, and the hair-breadth escapes of their companions and themselves, upon the tooth or bone of one of the monsters whom they have seen die. One of the grandest examples of such craft I have seen was upon a ship that patrolled the waters between the southern New Lands and San Borondon, executed upon a yard-long tooth. Its panoramic image was of the fearsome creature from which it was plucked, pictured “in a flurry” and pursued by a spate of skiffs from a finely-detailed schooner, but pierced with almost as many darts as the fabled Archemedon Wyrm slain by the sea-monks of San Borondon in Ontic antiquity. Though the creature’s vast powers must have been well-known long before the scriptural age, the natural history of the sea serpent has, since antiquity, been the opprobrium of zoologists and magi alike. It would be wearisome to detail all the distressing confessions of almost every philosopher who has approached this fell class of animals, even though perfectly aware of the difficulties of this subject. One of the most common debates within scientific circles turns around the question of whether the various sea serpents found around the World-Ocean, which range in size, coloration, fang dentation, etc., may constitute a single breed of creature, or a collection of separate species. The result of this experience is to confirm the opinion hazarded by Professor Zarxas, that there is but one known species of sea serpent. He says:—”It is not my intention, were it in my power, to enter into the inquiry as to the true method of dividing the hydracea into groups, families, genera, or species; but this I can assert in contradiction to Doctor Oucoumiche, and other authorities, that there is no more than one species of sea serpent, and this I say from having particularly noticed their external form, and also their manner and habits, in various parts of the world very distant from each other. The large full-grown male appears the same in every part, from New Lovegain to the Cassiterides, from the Cassiterides to the tip of Norumbega, from Norumbega to San Borondon; while their females coincide in every particular, having their young ones among them in the same order, and appearing similar to all others which I had seen in every respect, merely differing a little in color, length or fatness, according to the climate in which they were captured.”…
