How to Love the World More: Artist and Poet Rachel Hébert’s Breathtaking Catalogue of Gratitudes

Here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

Imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

A taste:

What do we say to longing?

If you have sat in the chill

of early morning bleakness

and watched as the deep blue

sighed and blushed, touched

by the warm curve of dawn

and pinker than pink then

apricot soft and spreading its

glow, you know. You know.

How

— in this dim parade of brutality —

might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light,

train our sights on

the rebellious good,

and work

to make it

truer.

Beneath the face

of the water,

wonder.

In dark woods,

a gate.

In the chapter

called lostness,

a friend.

All the help

we could not

yet see.

It cannot be always comfortable.

So love the thousand knives as they enter

and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws

of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled

roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Know you’re no sicker than the rest of us.

The big secret is this: No one else can brave you.

Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see

in this world we’re pressed into,

its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin —

our efforts, our angers.

For music.

For wings.

The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”

“No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:

In the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:

How does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

A quintessential Route 66 diner has been serving up Americana for nearly 100 years

The Ariston Cafe along Route 66 in Litchfield, Ill., has been a favorite for more than 90 years. Just past the front door, underneath the vintage neon signs that read "Ariston" and "Budweiser," is a diner staple: a glass case, full of sweet temptations. It took one of the Ariston's owners, Will Law, nearly a full minute to reel off all 12 of the day's choices.

"There's a peach crisp bread pudding with the vanilla bourbon sauce," he said. "Then, of course, a traditional cheesecake with or without cherries, and we have a chocolate delight, a lemon delight, a coconut delight."

They were all delightful to look at and the kind of classic American comfort desserts that you might crave while you're road-tripping on America's most famous highway. All of them — like everything else served at the Ariston — are still made in-house.

Litchfield isn't the most natural stop on Route 66; it's a sleepy town about an hour outside St. Louis. But the Ariston Cafe, which sits just across the road from the charming Litchfield Museum & Route 66 Welcome Center, has become an institution in its own right with its wooden chairs and cozy decor.

Travelers still flock to the Ariston, thanks to the internet and social media. The waitstaff says many visitors come in already knowing exactly what they intend to order based on what they've read and seen online.

Right by the front door there's a guest book for diners next to a basket of reading glasses to make reading and signing easier. Within just a few days, the Ariston has welcomed patrons from Australia, South Korea, Nicaragua and Germany, among other nations. And they come from all over the U.S. too.

Bob Dickson celebrated his 75th birthday with his wife, Ann, by traveling Route 66.

"I said to her, 'I would love to go out west to Los Angeles and bring Highway 66 all the way back to where we live,'" he said. "So we did that. We took 31 days, stopped every place you can imagine on and off the highway. We had a great time, an absolutely great time talking to people and just seeing the sights."

On this day's visit, they are just a couple of hours away from their home in Quincy, Ill., and they've stopped for a last celebratory lunch on their big trip. The menu offers so many choices, from patty melts to turkey clubs to pork chops and stuffed shrimp. They said this restaurant, with its throwback vibes and sprawling menu, encapsulates the spirit of their whole road trip.

"It was really adventurous and old fashioned and very joyful," Ann Dickson said.

Opinions run hot about what exactly is the oldest eatery along Route 66, but the Ariston Cafe claims to be the oldest continually operating restaurant on the highway.

Nick Adam is one of the Ariston's former owners. His father, Pete, founded it as a candy shop in 1924. Adam says his father was very young when he arrived in this country.

"He left when he was 10 to come to the United States," Adam explained. "He went back to Greece when he was 12, and then he came back to this country."

Pete Adam seems to have had big ambitions even back then: The shop's name, Ariston, means "the best" in Greek. In 1935, he moved it to its present location on Route 66. Then Nick and his wife, Demi, ran the restaurant for decades.

From first dates to engagements, Demi Adam said the Ariston Cafe has been a fundamental part of this community for decades.

"To be honest," she said, "there's nothing else like this around."

Eight years ago, when the Adams were ready to retire, they sold the restaurant to Will Law and his partners. Law said the Ariston's position as a place locals and visitors alike choose for the big moments in their lives remains unchanged.

"I can't tell you how many wedding proposals have happened in those booths," he said. "We have a couple from Iowa that will come back every year for their anniversary just to have dinner. I see a 50th anniversary at least once a week, if not 60, 65. How cool is that? And they want to share that with you."

In 2006, the Ariston Cafe was put on the National Register of Historic Places. It's another lasting reminder of what this restaurant that steps back in time can mean to visitors in the present.

13.8 billion years ago, what we know today as our observable Universe began with the most important origin event in cosmic history: the hot Big Bang. Once the Universe became filled with matter, antimatter, and radiation in an almost-perfectly uniform fashion, it expanded and gravitated in nearly perfect balance. As the Universe cooled, the matter and antimatter annihilated away, leaving a tiny, minuscule, but significant amount of matter behind. After 9.2 billion years, what would become our Solar System gradually began to form from a collapsing cloud of molecular gas, and after another 4.55 billion years or so, humanity first arose on planet Earth.

When we look out at the Universe from our perspective in the here-and-now, we only get a snapshot of all of existence: defined by the properties of the light, particles, and gravitational waves that we observe at the moment of their arrival. Based on all that we’ve seen, combined with our theories, frameworks, and models that reflect the fusion of those observations with the underlying laws of physics, we’ve come to understand the cosmos around us.

However, if things had been only a tiny bit different initially, the outcomes that resulted all throughout our Universe would have been altered dramatically. Here are five things that could have happened, but didn’t, that would have changed the course of our shared cosmic history.

1.) What if the Universe were actually perfectly uniform when it was born?

This one is not something that’s greatly appreciated: the Universe, as we know it, couldn’t have been born perfectly smooth. If we had possessed an exactly equal amount of matter-and-antimatter-and-radiation everywhere, at all locations in space, going all the way back to the earliest moments of the hot Big Bang, every point in the Universe would have experienced an equal gravitational force pulling on it in all directions. The idea of gravitational growth and collapse, which is required to make stars, galaxies, planets, humans, and the grand cosmic web, all relies on a set of initial imperfections to begin growin from.

Without any such seeds, you can’t get the desired end result of structure, including structures such as a star, galaxy, or something even larger. The only hope would then be something that originated from the quantum-scale fluctuations inherent to the nature of the Universe. Because we have quantum processes that cannot be avoided:

- inherent uncertainties in the positions and momenta of particles,

- inherent uncertainties between the energy in a system and the amount of time that passes,

- and exclusion rules that prevent certain particles from occupying identical quantum states,

some amount of imperfections will automatically arise even if there were none initially.

From these quantum processes, you’d expect the initial imperfections that the Universe was born with to arise at around the 1-part-in-10³⁵ level, which is an extremely tiny amount. For comparison, as informed by observations, our Universe was born with imperfections that arose at the 1-part-in-30,000 level. This, too, is small, and means that on average, our actual Universe was born uniform to within 99.997% precision. However, the imperfections that our actual Universe was birthed with are absolutely enormous compared to the tiny quantum fluctuations that arise from the mundane processes that occur today: more than 30 orders of magnitude larger.

Grateful for curious minds

Based on the way that imperfections grow in the Universe, it took somewhere around ~100 million years for the largest of the initial fluctuations that the Universe started off with to form the first stars. If the Universe would have been born with fluctuations that were 1-part-in-10,000,000 (ten million) instead, we’d very likely only be forming the first stars now. The reason is simple: gravitational growth takes a very long time unless you start from a substantially large seed, and only once the overdense regions become about twice as dense as the average density does gravitational growth start to meaningfully accelerate.

If our Universe were born exactly, perfectly uniform, then even by today, 13.8 billion years after the Big Bang, there would be no structure, no stars, and no interesting chemical reactions to speak of anywhere in the cosmos.

2.) What if the expansion rate and the effects of gravitation were less perfectly balanced?

This one is a bit tricky. We normally think of the Universe as a fairly stable place, but that’s only because there are two cosmic properties that have been so well-balanced for so long: the rate at which the Universe expands and the decelerating effects of all the matter and radiation in the Universe. Today, these two effects don’t match, and that’s why we say the expansion of the Universe is accelerating. The fact that there’s a third meaningfully energetic component to the Universe, dark energy, is what causes that mismatch, and therefore is what drives the current accelerated expansion of the cosmos.

However, for the first ~6 billion years of the Universe’s history, the expansion rate and the effects of matter-and-radiation didn’t just match, they matched so perfectly well that what we know of as dark energy would have been completely undetectable, even if a hypothetical alien civilization were to develop the exact tools we use today to measure the Universe. The farther back in time you go, the less important dark energy becomes relative to matter and radiation. And we can go back not just billions of years, but all the way back to the first tiny fraction-of-a-second after the hot Big Bang.…

Back in late 1944, two regiments of the 6th Marine Division were on Guadalcanal, training for an invasion of a target they didnât know yet, and they had more pressing matters on their minds: which of them had the better football team. The 4th and 29th Marines were loaded with former college stars, and according to Buzz Bissinger, whose 2022 book is the basis of Peter Bergâs new film, the 65 men who eventually played included three All-Americans and seven college captains, from Brown to Notre Dame to California.

On NPRâs Fresh Air, Bissinger did the 4th Regimentâs trash talk for them (âThis is the 4th Regiment. We are loadedâ), and the 29th, naturally, disagreed.

Christmas Eve on the Coral

The game got set for Christmas Eve 1944, and the Marines went at it like the Rose Bowl was coming to Guadalcanal. There were printed rosters, a public-address system, radio announcers, and regimental bands, Denver sportswriter Terry Frei reported in his 2003 account, which drew on interviews with surviving players. It was played on the 29thâs parade ground, which was covered in coral and gravel as well as dirt, and had no grass. The game was supposed to be touch football, but the Marines, being Marines, turned it into tackle. âFifteen hundred Marines came, drunk. No one cared. Gambling, no one cared,â Bissinger said, and no one was wearing pads or helmets.

The players included Wisconsinâs two-time All-American end Dave Schreiner, captain of the 4th; Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich, the first-round draft pick of the Cleveland Rams; Notre Dameâs 1942 captain, George Murphy; Schreinerâs Wisconsin teammate Bob Bauman; and John McLaughry, a former Brown star who had played for the New York Giants. Frei notes that the 4thâs backup quarterback was an East St. Louis native named Hank Bauer, who later played and managed in the major leagues. A Marine combat correspondentâs United Press dispatch called the whole thing âthe Mosquito Bowl football classic,â and the name stuck.

After all that, the score was 0-0. Thereâs even a dispute about the last play: Bissinger says a field goal was blocked, while Frei and History.com say the 4thâs quarterback, Bob Spicer, made an interception at the end. The Marines wanted a rematch, but the 4th Regimentâs commander, Alan Shapley, refused, telling them, as Bissinger put it, that if they were going to get killed or hurt, he wanted it to happen in combat and not in a football game. Since nobody won, all the bets were a push.

Okinawa

By the middle of March 1945, the division had shipped out, and on April 1, the Marines landed on Okinawa. The battle lasted 82 days, and 15 of the 65 Mosquito Bowl players were killed in it, according to History.com; Schreiner, Bauman, and Butkovich were among them. On May 15, Murphy led a platoon of the 29th up Sugar Loaf Hill, and after the men ran out of grenades, he ordered a withdrawal on his own initiative. The Armyâs official history of the campaign records what happened next: âCovering the men as they pulled back down the slope, Murphy was killed by a fragment when he paused to help a wounded Marine.â Schreiner was shot on June 20 and died the next day, hours before the island was declared secure. He was 24 years old.

That fall, Time ran a short piece on the divisionâs football players. âWhen it headed for the Pacific, the 6th Marine Division boasted enough football talent to line up three all-star teams,â it said. âNow, on the way back, the 6th would be hard-pressed to muster one full team.â

The Movie

Berg, who directed the movie version of Bissingerâs Friday Night Lights, co-wrote the new film with Mark L. Smith, according to Netflix. Netflixâs Tudum lists Nicholas Galitzine as McLaughry, Bill SkarsgÃ¥rd as Bauman, Ray Nicholson as Butkovich, and Tom Francis as Schreiner. item.description:

Why it is here: clear analysis of economic trends

Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers. With inflation fatigue, declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back?

This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering.

Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than what was expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates, consumer spending held up remarkably well.

I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way.

What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many people to keep up.

What resilience looks like

Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous.

Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands, shopping at off-brand and discount stores, or relentlessly hunting for deals. Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans.

“Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect, and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce.

These are both responses to the rising cost of living.

More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make some extra cash.

About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter – whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn extra discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn.

Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges.

According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the actual number of donors is dropping.

Shoppers are hitting the limit

Many consumers are now running out of levers to pull.

Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip, which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest.

One in four families are spending more than they make, as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago.

For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high. Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences. Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise.

And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now – with unemployment at 4.1% – is critical. If this healthy job market holds and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise, Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink – and hurt economic growth in the process.

That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady.

Whether it comes to this, it’s important to remember that the holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down?

Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers are facing challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 – but that’s far from a sure thing.

Why it is here: useful information on public domain

The public domain just keeps growing every New Yearâs Day, and Mental Floss has been keeping track of the latest additions, most recently with the class of 2025. This time, 1931 is the year that goes public, and that means we get two of the Universal monsters, Chaplinâs Tramp, a couple of Nancy Drew books, and the song Sam plays in Casablanca.

How the Rule Works

Works from 1931 are protected for 95 years, ending on December 31, 2026. However, there is a special provision for American works. As Dukeâs Center for the Study of the Public Domain notes, for U.S. works to be protected for the full 95 years, they must have been published with a copyright notice, and then the copyright must have been renewed after 28 years. So every work on this list was checked against the Copyright Officeâs renewal catalogs from 1958 and 1959, which have been scanned by the Internet Archive. Sound recordings from this period are on a different timeline. The 2018 Music Modernization Act extended the copyright on sound recordings first published between 1923 and 1946 by five years, meaning that recordings from 1926 will enter the public domain on January 1.

Frankenstein

Mary Shelleyâs monster is already in the public domain, of course. But James Whaleâs movie? Universal registered it on November 16, 1931, and then renewed it in 1959. Come January, Colin Clive screaming âItâs alive! Itâs alive!â is up for grabs, and so are the flat head and neck bolts that most of us picture when somebody mentions Frankenstein. The monster was played by a little-known actor named Boris Karloff after Bela Lugosi turned it down.

Dracula

Lugosi could afford to be picky because he was already the Count. Tod Browningâs Dracula was registered by Universal on February 2, 1931, and released across the country on Valentineâs Day. It became one of the studioâs biggest hits of the year, and some film historians even say it saved Universal from bankruptcy. It was renewed in December 1958.

City Lights

This one was written and directed by Charlie Chaplin, who registered it in his own name on February 1, 1931, and then renewed it himself in 1958. Itâs the story of the Little Tramp, who meets a blind flower girl who mistakes him for a rich guy, and then saves a drunk millionaire who treats him like a best friend until he gets sober and doesnât recognize him anymore. The movie goes free on January 1, 2027, but as Chaplinâs website points out, the Little Tramp is a trademark, so donât go selling any bowler-hat merch just yet.

The Public Enemy

Warner Bros. registered William A. Wellmanâs gangster picture on April 4, 1931. It took the top spot on Mental Flossâs list of best gangster movies as the role that defined James Cagneyâs career, and it was based on Beer and Blood, an unpublished novel by two former newspapermen. It was renewed in 1958, so Cagney shoving that grapefruit in Mae Clarkeâs face will soon be fair game.

Monkey Business

The Marx Brothersâ films have been going public at a rate of one movie a year: The Cocoanuts in 2025, then Animal Crackers in 2026, according to Duke. Paramountâs Monkey Business is up next. It was registered September 17, 1931, and renewed in December 1958, with Norman McLeod directing and the story credited to S.J. Perelman and Will B. Johnstone. Some film professor is probably already plotting a very cheap triple feature.

Sanctuary

William Faulknerâs As I Lay Dying went public on January 1, 2026, and Sanctuary comes a year later. Faulkner registered the novel on February 9, 1931, and renewed it himself on February 26, 1958. Thereâs a separate copyright on an introduction he added in 1932, which he renewed in 1959, so if youâre reprinting the book, leave out the preface until 2028.

The Good Earth

Pearl S. Buck registered The Good Earth on March 2, 1931, and renewed it in March 1958. Itâs the first book in her trilogy about the Wang family, followed by Sons and A House Divided, and according to the official Nobel Prize site, those books gave Buck her major literary breakthrough on the way to the 1938 prize for literature. Sons came out in 1932, so the Wang family saga goes free one book at a time.

The Glass Key

The novel version of The Maltese Falcon went public in 2026, according to Duke, and Dashiell Hammettâs next novel is right behind it. Hammett registered The Glass Key twice in 1931, once in January and once in April, and renewed it in October 1958. The author, it seems, liked to be sure.

Nancy Drew: The Secret at Shadow Ranch and The Secret of Red Gate Farm

The first four Nancy Drew books went public in 2026, and 1931 brings the next two. The Secret at Shadow Ranch was registered on January 28, 1931, and renewed in January 1959. The Secret of Red Gate Farm was registered on August 12, 1931, and its renewal credits Harriet S. Adams and Edna C. Squier as the authors behind the pen name, a reminder that Carolyn Keene never existed.

âAs Time Goes Byâ

Herman Hupfeld registered the words and music on July 28, 1931, and the copyright was renewed in July 1958. The song was more than a decade old when Casablanca premiered in November 1942 and made âPlay it, Sam. Play âAs Time Goes Byââ one of the American Film Instituteâs top movie quotes. The sheet music goes free on January 1, but Casablanca itself has to wait until 2038.

âMinnie the Moocherâ

This is only the composition going public, not the recordings, the same distinction Duke made for last yearâs songs. Callowayâs 1931 records are subject to the 100-year rule for sound recordings, so they remain protected through 2031.

When most of us imagine the 1920s, we might think of flapper dresses and the glittery parties of The Great Gatsby. Still, amid all the upheaval and change during this decade, families were very much living out their everyday lives in America.Â

During the â20s, rapid economic growth after World War I revved up consumer culture, and many families began buying cars, lighting their homes with electricity, and purchasing stock using credit. All this economic expansion would ultimately culminate in the Great Depression, but during the â20s, many families found themselves with access to more economic abundance than ever before. Radio

The first radio broadcast aired on Christmas Eve in 1906, and the technology experienced rapid expansion in the 1920s. In 1921 there were just five radio stations in America, but there were 606 by the end of the decade. During this time, radio became a âpervading and somewhat godlike presence,â E. B. White wrote in 1933, that brought news, entertainment, music, and advertising to even the most rural locations. Gathering around the radio became a family ritual, and these machines often occupied special places in living rooms. Radio stars became household names, broadcasts became key parts of mornings, evenings, and holidays, and far-flung, disconnected communities now had access to breaking news and the day's newest music, among other cultural currents.

Phonograph

Thomas Edison invented the tin-foil phonograph in 1877, and gramophones were introduced in the late 1880s. These machines made their way into family homes throughout the early 20th century, and by the mid-1920s, the majority of family homes had some kind of record player. The typical 1920s model was hand-cranked and was generally kept in cabinets or cases in the parlor.Â Many of the biggest hits of the day were novelty songs, though greats like Louis Armstrong and Mamie Smith also occupied key places in many people's record collections.

Icebox

Electric refrigerators had been invented by the 1920s, but they were too expensive for the average American family at the time and did not become popular until after World War II. Instead, most families kept perishable food in iceboxes, which were wooden cabinets that held blocks of ice in their upper chambers. An ice man would deliver fresh ice to homes multiple times per week, and families would regularly clear out the melted water from a pan on the floor.Â

Wood Stove

In the 1920s, most houses did not have central heating or wall insulation. Instead, families relied on fireplaces, oil and coal-powered heaters, or wood-burning stoves to make it through cold winters. Wood stoves worked better than fireplaces, but still required regular maintenance and lots of firewood. Nights could get bitterly cold after the wood burned down, so many people still relied on warm clothes to stay cozy on frigid evenings.

Washboard

Many of us might complain about laundry day today, but truthfully, our experiences have absolutely nothing on what it takes to wash clothes without a machine. Electric washing machines had been invented by the 1920s and some wealthy homes had them, but the majority of 1920s families still washed clothes by hand. âWash dayâ typically occurred once a week. Clothes would be scrubbed over a washboard before being rinsed and boiled in separate pots, then hung to dry. This had to be done on cold winter days as well as hot summer ones, and clothes would sometimes freeze on clotheslines. The day after was often set aside for ironing, which usually required another full dayâs labor.

Band-Aids

Band-aids were invented in 1920, though at the time they were handmade strips that users had to cut. Pre-cut bandages hit shelves in 1924, and they soon became a staple in 1920s cabinets. A typical â20s medicine cabinet might have also included Vaseline, aspirin, safety razors, and thermometers, as well as some more experimental itemsâsuch as chlorine gas bombs, which were canisters of chlorine gas that users believed could help with colds when released into a room.

Vacuum Cleaner

The 1920s saw a boom in vacuum cleaners, which were invented in the early 20th century. Vacuums were generally marketed to middle-class women, along with promises of freedom from the challenges of housework during an era when servants and maids had become much less common. In reality, this deviceâs popularity led to higher standards for cleanliness at home and created more work for many women. Before vacuum cleaners, rugs had typically been brought outside and beaten just once or twice a year, but vacuums (and advertisements that emphasized the dangers of dust and particles) helped create the expectation that women were responsible for single-handedly maintaining completely spotless homes.

Automobile

Cars exploded in popularity in the 1920s, transitioning from luxury items to everyday necessities. Major companies like Ford, Chrysler, and General Motors made cars more accessible to regular people thanks to the likes of Ford's iconic Model T. In turn, cars transformed American industry, creating huge numbers of manufacturing jobs, stoking urbanization, and redefining the food industry. They altered every aspect of life for many people, making travel and leisure activities more accessible and catalyzing many cultural shifts that would define the decades to come.

The Portuguese second-tier team hosting Celtic in Europe

S.C.U Torreense's league fixtures this season include meetings with the 'B' teams of Sporting, Benfica and Porto.

But the Portuguese second division club, located 35 miles north of Lisbon, are in this season's Europa League after stunning giants Sporting to win the Taca de Portugal in May.

"This is a landmark moment," Andre Sabino, the club's director of football and CEO told BBC Sport.

Torreense had never played a European home match before their 2-1 defeat by Sunderland in October and welcome Celtic to Leiria on Thursday (20:00 GMT).

They won at Norwegian side Lillestrom on their debut but lost heavily in Hungary against Ferencvaros before beating Ararat-Armenia last time out.

Managed by Luis Tralhao, whose brother Joao is an assistant to Jose Mourinho at Real Madrid, the club are hoping to do more than just make up the numbers.

"It is something extraordinary for Torreense. These are clubs with huge histories, strong identities and enormous European experience," Sabino added.

"To be able to share the same competition and compete against them is a privilege. But we don't want to simply participate. We want to compete."

'Something that won't happen again in Portuguese football'

Second-tier Beira-Mar played in the 1999-2000 Uefa Cup, although they were a top-flight team at the time of qualifying. But Torreense are the first team from the second division to qualify by winning the Taca de Portugal.

"The Portuguese Cup has been played since 1938 in its current model and it was the first time that a second division team won it," Portuguese football journalist and ex-Benfica goalkeeper Jose Delgado told BBC Sport.

"You can imagine when they could defeat a giant club like Sporting in the final, it was quite a surprise and for the city, it's something very, very special."

After beating Lillestrom, they have already exceeded the expectations of some. "I thought that Torreense could go through the Europa League with no points," added Delgado.

With Portugal ranked outside Uefa's top five leagues, every club in the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League has a responsibility to perform well to earn their nation important ranking points.

"For Portuguese football, everybody [thought it] was nice that a club like Torreense won the cup but also we had some concerns," said Delgado.

"The first game everybody thought that Torreense had no chance against Lillestrom and they won. It was quite a good surprise. But it's like a fairytale for Torreense because they are a small club."

A 150km round-trip for home matches

As their 2,431-capacity home at Estadio Manuel Marques does not pass Uefa's stadium criteria, they will instead face Celtic almost 47 miles away at the Municipal Stadium in Leiria.

"Obviously, it is not ideal," Sabino explained. "Playing at home should mean playing in your own stadium, in front of your own supporters and in the environment that represents your club.

"But at the same time, we understand the logistical and regulatory requirements involved in European competition.

"We have to look at the bigger picture. We are extremely grateful for the opportunity to compete in the Europa League and we will make Leiria feel as much like home as possible."

The additional travel has not deterred supporters from watching their beloved club face big European names.

"Our supporters and our people are what make a home, regardless of the kilometres. The response from our supporters has been fantastic," Sabino added.

"They understand that this is a historic moment for Torreense and they want to experience it with us.

"We hope to see Leiria filled with Torreense colours and feel that support from the first minute."

A Â£4.2m windfall

Torreense missed out on a return to Portugal's top division for the first time since 1991-92 after a 2-0 two-legged defeat by Casa Pia in a promotion/relegation play-off in May. And fell at the first hurdle in their defence of the Taca de Portugal.

But qualification for the Europa League's league phase guarantees a financial injection of at least 5m euros (Â£4.2m).

Every positive result and extra round reached adds more to that pot.

"For a club like Torreense, it is a very significant amount," Sabino explained. "It gives us an opportunity to strengthen the club in several areas and to accelerate projects that otherwise would naturally take much longer.

"However, we have to be very responsible. Success can create opportunities but it also creates responsibilities.

"Our objective is not simply to spend more because we have more resources. We want to invest intelligently, strengthen the structure of the club and create conditions for sustainable growth."

19 new recruits from 10 different countries

Torreense have made 19 new signings from across the globe for this season.

As well as turning to Portugal's top flight for five new recruits, other signings have come from France, Greece, Spain, Serbia, Portugal, Brazil, Denmark, Morocco and Germany. The majority from outside those countries' top leagues.

Of their 32-man senior squad, just four are Portuguese.

"It has been a very different challenge," Sabino explained. "European football changes the perception of the club and naturally makes Torreense more attractive to certain players, but it also increases expectations."

Last season, Torreense missed out on automatic promotion on goal difference before losing the play-off. This term they have won only two of their opening 10 league games and sit 13th.

With the overwhelming majority of football fans in Portugal supporting one of the 'big three' of Porto, Benfica and Sporting - Delgado says sometimes home fans even cheer for their more illustrious opponents when they visit.

"Right now I think that there is a great sympathy about Torreense, but I don't think they will get many more [fans] because of this presence," he added.…

Former England captain Ben Stokes says he hopes they win next year's Ashes 5-0, though he would not be drawn on Sandpapergate or the possibility of him making a comeback for the series.

Speaking to Sky Sports upon the launch of a new podcast he's presenting with former England team-mate Mark Wood called 'That's Not Cricket', Stokes hinted that he might have more to say on the saga dominating Australian cricket on that platform.

"It would be pretty bizarre for it not to be mentioned [on the podcast]", Stokes said. "It's all kicking off at the moment out there, isn't it?

"What Australia have going on there is far beyond anything we had to deal with [as a leadership group].

"I imagine Joe [Root] and Flem [Stephen Fleming] would be thinking, 'imagine if this happened three weeks before the Ashes next year, as opposed to now'."

'Root and Fleming will work really well together'

England's Test team enter into a new era under Root - who returned to the captaincy with a 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan following Stokes' international retirement - and Fleming, who begins as head coach with a three-Test tour of South Africa next month.

The series, against the reigning World Test Champions, serves as an ideal challenge for the new regime as they steel themselves for the visit of Australia next summer where they'll look to regain the Ashes for the first time since winning on home soil in 2015.

"I'm doing a Glenn McGrath here; I hope England win the Ashes 5-0," Stokes said. "I'm not saying they will, but I wish nothing but the best for them.

"I'm still an England cricket fan. I want the players, Joe and Flem to do well.

"There is no animosity whatsoever between any of us, there's no jealousy."

Stokes did add, however, that he was "surprised" to see Root take on the captaincy again, knowing first-hand how much the job takes out of you - as well as the toll it had taken on Root by the time he handed over the reins in 2022 after five years in the role.

"I was a little bit surprised, if I'm being honest, just because he knows what it's like and he's done so well as a player but also, knowing Joe, he feels like he can take the team from where it was and build on it again," Stokes said.

"It's an exciting time for someone to think like that and when Stephen Fleming got appointed, I thought 'these two are going to work really well together'.

"I did a lot of work with Flem in the IPL. He's a great man manager; everyone has already seen how he speaks, which is very impressive. I'm excited to watch them go about it."

Stokes: Everything after Ashes defeat was tough

Stokes' time as Test captain and as an England cricketer came to an end with a 2-1 series defeat to New Zealand, which was on the heels of a disastrous 4-1 Ashes drubbing in Australia during the winter.

"I was in the right headspace for the Ashes," Stokes reflected. "It was all after that. Before the Ashes, I was so confident.

"Everyone was fit, firing and ready to go. Fans and pundits were all confident, and Australia weren't confident, so we couldn't have been in a better place going out there.

"But emotion and the feeling of what you think is going to happen is completely different to getting out there in the heat of the battle. Everything after that was tough."

Stokes added: "Unfortunately, to do that role, you have to immerse yourself in it, have to throw yourself into it.

"For all the positive stuff that comes with it, there is a negative effect that can flow over into your home life and your family.

"I think every England captain will have that. I don't think there is anything you can do.

"You can try your hardest, but when you do that role you just have to do it. I don't think you are doing the role justice if you take it lightly.

"I always felt on as England captain. Now I can just be Ben, not Ben Stokes captain of the England cricket team. Looking back, it's not really a healthy place to be at."

As well as still playing for his county side Durham - helping them clinch promotion back to Division One of the County Championship - and an upcoming stint with the Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League, Stokes is using his newfound freedom to venture into the world of podcasting.

"I have been in the public eye for so long but people who don't know me probably only know 10, 15, 20 per cent of what I am actually like," he said. "That is the exciting thing: I now get a chance to say what I want to be going out.

"I don't feel like you're always necessarily able to give that full account of yourself as a person, because you're wary of upsetting people. The only person I can upset now is myself.

"It's really exciting and I can't wait to get going. We've got a lot to talk about and a lot to say."

'Laughing gas has ended careers' - so how common is it in football?

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

What is nitrous oxide?

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16â24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

Is it widely used by footballers?

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

- Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

'The worst thing you want to be using as a sportsperson'

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.…

The move to introduce a second semi-final has not been directly influenced by the arrival of external investment, though it has been welcomed by owners.

A primary motivation has come from a desire to maximise the competitiveness of matches played in the latter stage of the group phase.

The Hundred group stage is relatively short â only eight matches per team â meaning the margin between qualifying or missing out on the play-offs can be thin.

Los Angeles controlled the ball for 23:45 in the second half, squeezing the life from the Packers inside a lively SoFi Stadium for their Thanksgiving Eve match-up.

The Rams did it behind Corum, whose 32 carries were the most in the NFL this season and the most by any Rams running back in McVay's 10-year career. Corum had 25 carries for 161 yards in the second half alone while Los Angeles stayed in control.

Norse Atlantic Airways appears to be no more.

The Norway-based long-haul budget airline cancelled all flights late on Wednesday, its website and the flight tracking website FlightRadar24 show.

Pakistan International Airlines, which contracts Norse to operate select flights, said Wednesday evening on X that Norse had suspended operations "without prior notice."

A Norse spokesperson did not respond to requests for comment. However, in a statement Wednesday morning, the airline warned that its financial situation was "critical" and said its continued operation was "dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs."

Norse flew just one U.S. route at the time of its shut down: Orlando International Airport (MCO) to London's Gatwick Airport (LGW), schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show.

During the prime summer months, Norse also seasonally flew from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Athens International Airport (ATH) in Greece, LGW and Rome's Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci International Airport (FCO).

At its peak in 2024, Norse served five U.S. destinations, including Las Vegas's Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), from gateways in Europe.

The apparent collapse of Norse comes at a challenging time for airlines. Jet fuel is at historic highs, spiking after Iran war and other conflicts. Geopolitical tensions have closed significant swaths of airspace, including Russia and significant portions of the Middle East. And, high interest rates have pushed the cost of capital for any business to the highest levels in years.

Luis Gallego, the CEO of International Airlines Group that owns British Airways and Iberia, told the Financial Times in October that smaller airlines would struggle this winter due to the those financial headwinds.

Norse was one of the last airlines trying to make long-haul, low-cost work between the U.S. and Europe. Play Airlines, which attempted the same strategy via a connecting hub at Iceland's Keflavik International Airport (KEF), shut down in September 2025. And both Norse and Play were formed following the retrenchment and collapse of previous attempts; Norse from Norwegian Air's withdrawal from the market in 2021 and Play from the ashes of WOW Air that shut down in 2019.

Only independent French Bee and the budget arms of the larger European airline groups, including Discover, Level and Edelweiss Air, continue to offer lower-cost transatlantic flights.

item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Recently, our Georgetown team has been inundated with media requests for commentary on allegations involving the exposure of Nvidia chip technology and the implications for U.S. national security. These inquiries typically focus on how China’s intelligence services conduct espionage and what can be done to counter them.

We do not discount this threat. Espionage, cyber intrusions, and other clandestine activities are longstanding features of China’s efforts to acquire foreign technology. But our research over more than a decade suggests that these activities account for only a fraction of China’s overall foreign technology acquisition effort – probably not the largest fraction, and arguably not the most consequential.

Rather, China has created a whole-of-nation ecosystem that operates through a combination of legal transactions, illicit activities, and what we call “extralegal” transfers: arrangements whose details are unavailable to outside observers and whose legality cannot readily be established.

Because these less visible practices lack the sensational appeal of conventional espionage, they rarely receive comparable attention. The result is a distorted public understanding of China’s technology acquisition system and a misallocation of the resources intended to counter it.

Beyond Conventional Espionage

China’s pursuit of foreign technology is neither new nor mysterious. Since the founding of the People’s Republic in 1949, Beijing has operated an elaborate infrastructure for identifying foreign technological advances, accessing them, and adapting them for domestic use.

The enterprise includes government ministries, scientific research institutions, commercial entities, technology transfer centers, professional associations, overseas laboratories, and programs designed to recruit scientists and engineers with specialized expertise.

Its antecedents extend further back, to China’s 19th-century efforts to acquire Western technology while preserving its domestic political and social institutions. Successive Chinese governments have formalized these efforts. The objective is not simply to copy inventions, but to leverage the knowledge to produce commercially and strategically useful results.

For analytical purposes, we distinguish among three broad categories of foreign technology acquisition.

Legal transfers include purchases of technology, foreign company acquisitions, joint research, investments in startups, overseas laboratories, university collaborations, and the recruitment of scientific personnel. These transactions are not inherently improper. Yet a transaction can be legal while also being a strategic risk.

Illegal transfers include traditional espionage, cyber theft, violations of nondisclosure agreements, theft of trade secrets, alleged “honey pot” operations, and other activities prohibited by law. These are the practices most familiar to the public, which media queries most frequently address – as in the case of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.

Extralegal transfers involve arrangements in which foreign technical knowledge is conveyed through channels that are not necessarily illegal but frequently opaque. Examples are undisclosed research affiliations, subsidized consulting, dual appointments, and the work of intermediaries whose relationships with China’s government are not apparent.

These categories are not exclusive. An otherwise legitimate collaboration may involve undisclosed conflicts of interest, while a commercial acquisition may be entirely lawful yet raise significant national security concerns.

Our concern is that the second category attracts disproportionate attention, while the first and third may facilitate transfers of equal or greater strategic consequence.

The Machinery Behind the Transfers

The scale and institutional character of China’s acquisition efforts distinguish them from isolated acts of industrial espionage.

One component is China’s science and technology intelligence (科技情报, STI) system. This network collects, analyzes, and distributes foreign technical information to domestic research and industrial organizations. Its civilian institutions include the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China, complemented by specialized organizations serving particular industries and defense requirements.

Another component is the ubiquitous “talent programs” – a network of organizations that identify and recruit overseas technical expertise. Chinese national and local authorities have sponsored numerous programs offering research funding, salaries, laboratory facilities, and other incentives to scientists and engineers working abroad.

Some arrangements involve permanent relocation to subsidized “commercialization centers.” Others permit researchers to maintain positions overseas while executing projects or consulting assignments in China. These include so-called “dual-base” (两个基地) arrangements, through which an individual may sustain professional activities in two countries.

Participation in such programs or in their global analogs – the Sino-U.S. (or Japanese, German, etc.) “professional associations” – does not by itself establish misconduct. That depends on the nature of the work, the information transferred, and whether participants comply with applicable disclosure requirements and contractual obligations.

Unlike a clandestine intelligence operation, much of this infrastructure is publicly acknowledged in Chinese government documents and institutional announcements. Its strategic significance lies not in secrecy alone, but in its organization, persistence, and cumulative effects.

It is November 26 yet again, the anniversary of the 2008 Mumbai attacks. It’s a day when India not only relives one of the darkest chapters in its fight against terror but also has an opportunity to reflect back on how the fight against terror has evolved over time.

From a passive and often submissive strategy to a bold and highly kinetic strategy of “zero tolerance to terror,” the journey has been long but determined. A strong political resolve has aptly backed the armed forces in its sustained fight to dismantle the terror ecosystem, choke the support system, and bring terrorist forces to their knees, decisively. A brief glimpse of this was demonstrated during India’s response to the Pahalgam terror attack, which involved 88 hours of precision strikes into Pakistan in Operation Sindoor from May 7-10, 2025.

In recent weeks, another significant success was achieved in India’s fight against terror. On November 19, while addressing a counterterrorism conference in Delhi, India’s Home Minister Amit Shah hailed the security forces for eliminating the last known home-grown terrorist, Latif Bhat. Shah claimed that, with this success, the entire Kashmir has become free from India-born terrorists, marking a major milestone in India’s fight against terrorism. He added that India needs to further strengthen the concept of a proactive offensive approach in its counterterrorism policy, with a greater emphasis on enhancing structural and operational capabilities, to continue on this path.

As per data maintained by the South Asia Terrorism Portal, the number of terrorists killed in the current year is down to 25 from a high of 3,005 in 2001 and 1,232 in 2008. Similarly, casualties among the Indian security forces have dropped to four this year from highs of 883 in 2001 or 366 in 2008. Civilian casualties too have seen a drastic reduction with only two fatalities recorded this year against 1,508 in 2001 and 915 in 2008.

Does this mean that India has all but won its fight against terror? Does it mean that India can now focus more of its resources and thoughts on ever increasing threats on the conventional front? Has India’s multilayered counterterror strategy finally delivered the knock-out blow to cross border terror? Most of these questions do not have simple and binary answers and premature celebrations could undo years of hard work and sacrifices made by the armed forces.

A look back at how India’s counterterror strategy has evolved may offer answers to some of these questions.

Early Years of Terror Attacks: India’s Weak Response

Although the 26/11 terror attack in the financial capital of India, Mumbai, is often called India’s 9/11, India’s fight against terror truly started when cross-border terror from Pakistan commenced in Kashmir in early 1990s. Despite previous evidence, including captured documents, the direct role of Pakistan was first exposed with the hijacking of IC-814, an Indian Airlines flight, on December 24, 1999. Under huge public and international pressure – and also facing a lack of viable politico-military options – India agreed to release Pakistan based terrorists like Ahmed Omar Sheikh and Masood Azhar in exchange for over 160 civilian hostages.

The attack on the Indian Parliament in Delhi by Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), a Pakistan based terrorist group, on December 13, 2001 outraged India and led to a large-scale military mobilization under Operation Parakaram. Once again, under tremendous international pressure, especially as both countries had recently acquired nuclear weapons, the two-year stand-off finally ended without any direct punishment to Pakistan.

There were other terror attacks too, like the 2002 Akshardham Temple Attack, the 2006 Varanasi serial bomb blasts, or the German Bakery Blast in 2010 in Pune. In October 2005, 59 people were killed in serial blasts that rocked popular Delhi markets of Sarojni Nagar and Paharganj. Again, in September 2008, months before the Mumbai 26/11 attack, multiple blasts rocked commercial spaces of Delhi including Connaught Place, Greater Kailash and Karol Bagh. On September 7, 2011, a briefcase bomb exploded outside the Delhi High Court, killing 12 people, claimed by a terror group Harkat-ul-Jihad Islami (HUJI), affiliated with al-Qaida and largely based in Pakistan.

However, the 26/11 terror attack was nothing like anything seen before or since. Ten heavily armed terrorists, trained and dispatched from Pakistan through a maritime route, struck the heart of Mumbai. Over the next 60 hours, they attacked multiple locations, including the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, the Oberoi-Trident, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Nariman House, and Cama Hospital. By the time the siege ended, 166 people had lost their lives, including foreign nationals and security personnel. The attack was a sad reflection of India’s preparedness to fight terror, and the sea route taken by the terrorists exposed yet another major gap in India’s strategy for fighting terror.

In all these cases and many more, India failed to respond directly and decisively against Pakistan, despite conclusive proof of its direct support in these attacks. How and when did India change its strategy?

The Kinetic Strategy

The swearing-in of the Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led government in May 2014 had a significant effect on India’s counterterror strategy. As the Modi government consolidated its power, the counterterror strategy too acquired a more muscular form. item.title: How Can Australia Secure Its Future?
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

This week, Australian Foreign Minister Senator Penny Wong delivered a major foreign policy speech to the Australian Senate. The speech was titled “Securing Australia’s future in a changing world,” and it sought to outline how Australia can navigate and protect its interests amid the major geopolitical shifts that are currently taking place. In particular, she highlighted how Australia will continue to place the United States at the center of its security architecture, despite the major ideological shifts that have occurred under the Trump administration.

Wong identified six shifts that are currently driving the global environment.

The first is the rising threat and use of force and coercion, with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine the clearest case, but also China militarizing disputed features within the South China Sea. Following this is the second shift: great powers have rethought what they want from the international system and how they pursue it. Washington is reshaping how it thinks about its interests and Beijing is attempting to reshape the Indo-Pacific around its own interests.

The third shift relates to stronger middle powers, like India and Indonesia, alongside Japan and South Korea, bringing their economic, diplomatic, and military weight into the Indo-Pacific. It is a redistributing of power. The number of middle powers has expanded since the end of the Cold War and this is creating a new source of power on its own.

The fourth shift is that trade, investment, and supply chains that were once a constraint on conflict are now being deliberately used as levers of pressure. This is related to the fifth shift that technology is changing the nature of economic and strategic power. This is happening not only through emerging technologies related to energy, but also AI, which is disrupting systems faster than anything before it, and the foreign interference it enables is cheaper, faster and harder to spot.

The sixth shift Wong identified is that countries are now finding it harder to act together. Multilateral institutions are waning in both resources and trust, and consensus on any major issue is becoming more difficult to create.

In response to these shifts, Wong rejected both fatalism and nostalgia. Her answer is an Australian foreign policy that is active, adaptive, and ambitious, one built upon Four R’s: region, relationships, rules, and resilience.

While Australia has sought to expand and deepen its other relationships, Australia’s central security pillar remains its alliance with the United States. To many in Australia looking at the ideological and behavioral shifts of the U.S. under Donald Trump, this may be perplexing and disappointing.

Australia’s approach to this turn in Washington has been to muddle through. Wong acknowledged these ideological shifts, but stated that it doesn’t alter the fundamentals of U.S. power: its economy, its military, and its indispensable role in Indo-Pacific stability. Australia’s position is to convince Washington that the final point especially is in its interests, as it is central to Australia’s.

But Wong also said that the United States is a “vigorous democracy” able to remake itself and the direction of its foreign policy post-Trump is unknown. Canberra’s calculation has been that there will be a “swingback” following Trump’s presidency. The recent midterm results lend support to that calculation.

Regardless of how erratic the White House may currently be, Wong acknowledged that there are still a great number of assets that the alliance provides. It gives Australia advanced technology and intelligence it couldn’t acquire alone, and it strengthens Australia’s capability to help deter aggression in the region. The United States remains the largest source of foreign investment in Australia, and the critical minerals framework signed by the two countries last year is pivotal to Australia’s future prosperity.

Wong pushed back on those who say that Australia should abandon the alliance because of Trump’s behavior. The alliance is bigger than the current occupant of the White House, and leaving it behind would give up a central source of strategic weight just when Australia needs every source of influence it can get. It would mean fewer choices, more vulnerability, and less capacity to help sustain a regional balance that protects sovereignty. The reality for Australia is that there is nothing comparable to the alliance that would protect Australia’s interests any better.

However, this does not mean Australia should be solely reliant upon that alliance. Wong highlighted that Australia has created the Treaty on Common Security with Indonesia and enhanced security ties with the Philippines, Singapore, and Malaysia. item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

Two months ago, as concerns about AI safety dominated American headlines, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng met in New York. Seven weeks earlier, more than 1,100 researchers and executives at leading AI labs had signed a petition asking the U.S. government to support an international effort to “deliberately pace the frontier.” An individual lab slowing progress would do nothing to stop other labs from racing ahead. All American labs slowing down would do nothing to slow Chinese labs. Only a China-U.S. agreement could end the race dynamics.

The September meeting between the two ministers took the first fitful steps toward cooperation. Both sides agreed to formalize a “U.S.-China AI Dialogues” process, to set up an “incident line” for AI events with national security implications, and to begin developing protocols for agreeing on the leading AI dangers. They also agreed to hold their next round of talks in Shenzhen in November.

That was widely seen as referencing the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which both Bessent and He attended. But no dialogue between the two took place.

The intervening two months have seen both sides pulled away from cooperation, with China moving to restrict exports of its AI technology and the U.S. administration embroiled in a scandal over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Despite the setback, He and Bessent are both likely to attend the G20 summit in Florida from December 18-19, providing another chance for progress on cooperation.

Since their meeting in September, neither side has announced concrete measures to implement any of the three planks. Instead, both the United States and Chinese governments have taken steps to limit each other’s use of technology. In October, the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), over which He wields considerable influence, and the Ministry of Science and Technology published a draft revision of the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export that adds 23 AI technologies spanning large models, agents, compute clusters, and information processing. Should that draft be finalized, it could significantly reduce U.S. access to Chinese model technology just as American firms are increasingly using those models.

Bessent, meanwhile, is near the center of the fallout from revelations involving Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China, whose former executive Alice Huang reportedly had a longstanding affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. In a rare public dispute between Cabinet members, Bessent faulted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick for failing to add Megaspeed to the Entity List, a step he said Treasury and other agencies had favored for months.

The Monday before the APEC summit, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule, which BIS said was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, to curb Chinese remote access to U.S.-built chips in third-country data centers. MOFCOM responded in terse language to the decision, with a spokesperson declaring the rule “deviates from the important consensus reached by the two heads of state… China is strongly dissatisfied with this and firmly opposes it.”

Neither the Americans nor the Chinese issued an official explanation of why He and Bessent failed to meet in Shenzhen, as neither ever officially confirmed the meeting would take place (no official confirmation preceded the September meeting either). Sensitivity over the Huang affair, tension over new restrictions, or simply reprioritization may all have played a role.

But the relationship between the two negotiation leads seems to remain on solid footing. The AI safety side conversation in September was part of a larger discussion of economic cooperation focused on implementing an agreement reached in Busan in October 2025, under which China paused its rare earth export controls and pledged to buy American agricultural goods in exchange for U.S. tariff relief. After Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spoke with He on the same topic earlier this month, China extended its suspension of rare earth export controls and the US extended 178 tariff exclusions on Chinese goods.

The following week, Bessent spoke at the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations gala, where he was optimistic about China-U.S. cooperation on AI. The secretary said he expects the two sides to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before release and that they are “establishing a direct channel to ensure that either nation can promptly alert the other to serious incidents involving its SI [super intelligence, the administration’s term for AI] models.”

Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, for their part, briefly discussed AI and “agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions,” according to Bessent. While nothing suggests that statement will turn into a formal agreement, the continued discussion of AI safety gives hope that Bessent and He’s “AI dialogues” could restart at the G20 summit next month.

A sideline discussion there could name the negotiators responsible for ironing out the details of an incident line: defining “serious incident,” determining which agency or official is responsible for both initiating and receiving notifications, and confirming that the hotline is operational.…

item.title: Koizumi Shinjiro Is the Defense Whisperer That Japan Needs
item.description:
