Why it is here: original reporting, clear prose

How many countries can say that their defense minister hosts a leading podcast? While some politicians around the world appear as guests on popular programs, Koizumi Shinjiro juggles his duties as Japan’s sitting defense minister while releasing biweekly episodes. “Shinjiro Koizumi’s Podcast,” as it is titled, regularly ranks among Japan’s top three political podcasts, covering everything from the Self-Defense Forces’ (SDF) counterpiracy operations in Djibouti to his personal ginger pork recipe.

Through this platform and his broader public persona, Koizumi is gradually demystifying Japan’s defense establishment and helping the Japanese public make sense of what may be the country’s most complex security environment since World War II. In doing so, he is fostering a long-overdue, more informed public conversation about Japan’s defense policy.

Koizumi’s podcast did not begin with defense issues. Until October 2025, the program reflected his priorities as Japan’s agriculture minister – or self-declared “rice minister” – tasked with stabilizing rice prices. While he may not yet be Japan’s most seasoned defense official, Koizumi possesses what many of his predecessors in Cabinet posts have lacked: a gift for communication, good looks, youthful energy, and a charismatic personality reminiscent of his father, former Prime Minister Koizumi Junichiro. These qualities make him a prime intermediary between Japan’s opaque bureaucracy and the public, with the podcast offering an approachable medium for engagement.

The Japanese public most commonly associates the SDF with emergency response, dispatched in the event of an earthquake, flood, or other disaster at home or abroad. They are highly competent in this arena, delivering supplies and conducting search and rescue with remarkable speed and coordination. However, viewing the SDF primarily through the lens of disaster relief risks overshadowing what defending Japan may require of them – or the decisions the public must weigh about their capabilities and deployment.

Most of the Japanese public views the SDF favorably – 93.5 percent – making the public opinion climate conducive to fostering a better understanding of their actual responsibilities and Japan’s evolving defense priorities. Koizumi has pried open that door by showcasing the SDF’s various activities, including live-fire drills, joint exercises with the United States and other militaries, and participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations. In doing so, he highlights their strategic importance and the real sacrifices made by SDF personnel. He occasionally shares messages from listeners who say his podcast has deepened their appreciation for the SDF, with some even reporting that it has inspired them or family members to enlist.

A similar pattern could help raise awareness of wider defense issues. In a geopolitical climate marked by China’s rapid military buildup, the possibility of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait, an unpredictable nuclear-armed North Korea, and growing uncertainty about the United States’ security commitment, Japan has no shortage of challenges on its doorstep.

Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s administration has taken meaningful steps to bolster Japan’s defenses, including a push to revise the three strategic documents – the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program – by the end of this year. Defense spending may be hiked from just under 2 percent to 3.5 percent of GDP over the next five years, in line with updated U.S. demands of its allies. Perhaps even more stirring has been Takaichi’s suggestion that there may be “room to discuss” rewording Japan’s third non-nuclear principle of prohibiting the introduction of nuclear weapons into the country. She has also indicated that the SDF’s potential acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines was under serious consideration, a move that would challenge the current legal framework governing the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

These developments echo Koizumi’s recent calls to break the taboo on debating nuclear weapons. In a country strongly tied to its pacifist tradition, the Takaichi administration’s position departs from the general public sentiment, which firmly supports upholding the three non-nuclear principles. And while Koizumi, on his own, is unlikely to move the needle on this sensitive issue, he is perhaps the best candidate among Japan’s high-ranking officials to facilitate its public discussion.

A prerequisite to seriously broaching the nuclear weapons debate, however, is greater public awareness of the security threats Japan faces. This is also crucial if the Takaichi administration is to realize its most ambitious goal of constitutional revision, which would require not only approval by both Diet chambers but also a national referendum.

Polling shows that the Japanese public overwhelmingly sees China as the biggest national security threat. A full grasp of the security reality, however, requires not only identifying adversaries but also recognizing the importance of forging closer partnerships with like-minded neighbors like South Korea. Although relations with Seoul remain complicated by deep-rooted historical issues, Koizumi frequently shares insights from his diplomatic engagements, speaking positively about his interactions with his South Korean and other counterparts. Such glimpses may help improve public perceptions of these partners and convey their strategic value over time.

Koizumi’s podcast avoids the jargon and over-formality often found in political commentary, inviting listeners to contemplate the future of Japan’s security rather than be lectured. The sincerity with which he repeatedly expresses his appreciation for the SDF and the civil servants in his ministry has proven to resonate with listeners.…

There may be a ton of Black Friday deals on electronics, toys, and gadgets out there, but don't get your hopes up if you're looking for a PlayStation 5. Not only are they not discounted, but the combination of international chip shortages, high demand caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, and the general holiday shopping frenzy has also made it nearly impossible to purchase a new, unbundled PlayStation 5 at any price—nearly impossible, but not impossible.

Major retailers are fresh out of PlayStation 5 consoles

Whether you're looking for a PlayStation 5 Digital Edition, a PS5 with a disc drive, or the flagship PlayStation 5 Pro, you won't find them at major online retailers. PlayStation Direct lists all three consoles as "currently unavailable." Best Buy suggests making an account with them to "improve your odds" of getting one. I can't find a listing for a new PS5 on Amazon either.

You still have some options for obtaining a PS5, but none of them are great. Many refurbished PS5s are selling for well above the list price of a new unit. There are some bundled, special editions available, but you'll likely be paying a ton for those. If you're willing to get your hands dirty by dealing with the wild west of Facebook Marketplace, you might be able to track down a used PlayStation 5 at a reasonable price, but approach with extreme caution.

How to get the best price on a refurbished PlayStation 5

If you're looking for a refurbished PlayStation 5, the best way to avoid a headache is to focus on who did the refurbishing. Buying refurbished electronics directly from a manufacturer is generally safer than buying from a third party, and in this case, it's cheaper too. PlayStation Direct is offering a "Certified Refurbished PlayStation 5 Console" for the relatively reasonable price of $519, while a refurbished Slim sells for $499. But if you're in the market, I'd lock it in quick: PlayStation Direct is already out of refurbished PS5 Pros.

Amazon's Renewed program has some strict requirements for third parties to stay in the program, like keeping defect rates under 0.8%, but refurbished PlayStation 5s are going for a premium on Amazon at the moment. A quick look at the site reveals that the price of a refurbished PlayStation 5 is hovering near $900; a refurbished PS5 Slim will run you somewhere around $750, and the current average price of a refurbished PS5 Pro has ballooned to over $1,700. These are well above the retail prices of $649 for the standard version, $599 for the digital version, and $899 for the flagship Pro version of the PlayStation 5.

Buying a bundled PlayStation 5 console is costly as well

There are some bundled versions of the console listed for sale online too. If you buy one of these, you're getting a new console and some other piece of hardware or a game, but there's a ton of upcharge at the moment. Buying a PlayStation 5 on the used market

By far the largest used market for anything in the U.S. is Facebook Marketplace, including PlayStation 5s. I checked out my local Marketplace, and there are a lot of listings for the console within a 40-mile radius of Los Angeles. I've bought and sold a fair number of things on Marketplace with no problems beyond the occasional flaky person, and I've written a list of hacks for the service, but I wasn't covering a "shortage buying" situation like this. Scams tend to rise with demand, so when I see a listing for a $150 PS5 console (that contains the text "$250 or best offer"), I'm suspicious. It could have been posted by someone who doesn't know what they have, but I wouldn't count on it. If you're buying a PS5 on Marketplace, check the model and generation details very carefully against the actual item. Make sure the seller is offering what you want and not a PlayStation 4 with PS5 games. Verify how it was stored and the condition it's in. But it ultimately can come down to vibes: Don't let your desire to score a PlayStation 5 get in the way of your gut check about the seller or situation.
